Female cases represented about 52% of all infections, and 868 (2.65%) of cases occurred among Indigenous individuals, with higher proportions in the 20‐29 age group, while infants under one year and persons aged 60+ had specific percentages for each virus. The highest case counts were observed in the municipalities of Manaus, Tabatinga, and São Paulo de Olivença.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors conclude that preventing uncontrolled arboviral emergence in Indigenous Amazonas requires health surveillance, cultural respect, and territorial protection beyond the traditional urban model.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform targeted surveillance, culturally appropriate prevention, and territorial protection strategies for Indigenous communities to mitigate arboviral risks.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The retrospective descriptive design based on surveillance bulletin data may suffer underreporting and limited demographic detail, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

papers.title_zh: 登革热、 Zika 病毒和基孔肯雅热在亚马逊土著人群中的流行病学分析:2021-2025 年情况概述
papers.source_body_en: Introduction: The spread of arboviruses considered urban into Indigenous territories reflects a critical scenario of socio-environmental vulnerability and epidemiological transition. Objective: To describe cases of Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika among the Indigenous population in Amazonas. Methodology: A retrospective descriptive study analyzing data from the epidemiological bulletin of the Amazonas Health Surveillance Foundation (FVS-RCP) covering the years 2021 to 2025. Results: Between January 2021 and December 2025, 32,730 cases of emerging arboviruses were reported in the state of Amazonas; of these, 31,401 (95.94%) were Dengue (DENV), 660 (2.02%) were Zika virus (ZIKV) infections, and 669 (2.04%) were Chikungunya (CHIKV). Considering the three arboviruses collectively, a slight female predominance was observed, accounting for approximately 52% of cases. Of the total notifications, 868 cases (2.65%) occurred in Indigenous individuals across all age groups, with the highest concentration in the 20–29 age range; this group represented 17% of DENV cases, 20% of ZIKV cases, and 16% of CHIKV cases. Cases were also identified among infants under one year of age (2% for DENV, 6% for ZIKV, and 2% for CHIKV) and among individuals aged 60 or older (6%, 4%, and 6%, respectively). Among Amazonas municipalities with significant Indigenous populations, Manaus, Tabatinga, and São Paulo de Olivença recorded the highest numbers of arbovirus cases, highlighting the occurrence of these infections across various age groups and territories within the state. Conclusion: To prevent the uncontrolled emergence of arboviral diseases among Indigenous populations in Amazonas, strategies must go beyond the urban model, integrating tailored health surveillance, respect for local culture, and territorial protection.
papers.abstract_zh: 引言:蚊媒病毒从城市地区传播到原住民领地反映了社会环境脆弱性和流行病学转变的关键情景。目的:描述亚马逊州原住民人群中登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的病例情况。方法:回顾性描述性研究,分析2021年至2025年期间亚马逊州卫生基金会(FVS-RCP)流行病学通报中的数据。结果:2021年1月至2025年12月,亚马逊州报告了32,730例新兴蚊媒病毒感染病例;其中31,401例(95.94%)为登革病毒(DENV)感染,660例(2.02%)为寨卡病毒(ZIKV)感染,669例(2.04%)为基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)感染。考虑到这三种蚊媒病毒,女性病例占比较高,约占总病例的52%。在所有年龄段中,共有868例(2.65%)病例发生在原住民人群中,其中最高比例集中在20–29岁年龄段;该年龄段占DENV病例的17%、ZIKV病例的20%和CHIKV病例的16%。病例也出现在1岁以下婴儿中(DENV为2%,ZIKV为6%,CHIKV为2%)以及60岁及以上人群中(DENV为6%,ZIKV为4%,CHIKV为6%)。在亚马逊州原住民人口较多的市镇中,马瑙斯、塔巴廷加和圣保罗德奥利维尼亚记录了最多的蚊媒病毒感染病例,突显了这些感染在州内不同年龄组和领地中的发生情况。结论:为了防止亚马逊州原住民人群中蚊媒病毒疾病不受控制地出现,防控策略必须超越城市模式,结合适合当地情况的健康监测,尊重当地文化,并加强领地保护。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 蚊媒病毒向土著地区扩散凸显了关键的社会环境脆弱性和流行病学转变,产生了记录该人群疾病发生情况的必要性;本研究旨在描述亚马逊地区土著人群中登革热、基孔肯雅热和寨卡病毒的病例。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对2021-2025年监测数据的回顾性描述性分析,土著人群占32,730例总报告中的868例(2.65%)。
analysis_zh.methods: 一项回顾性描述性研究分析了2021年至2025年的监测通报数据,未进行实验干预,以描述虫媒病毒病例特征。
analysis_zh.main_results: 2021年1月至2025年12月期间,亚马逊州报告了32,730例虫媒病毒病例,其中登革热占95.94%,寨卡病毒占2.02%,基孔肯雅病毒占2.04%。女性病例约占所有感染病例的52%,其中868例(2.65%)发生在土著居民中,20-29岁年龄组的比例较高,而1岁以下婴儿和60岁以上人群则每种病毒有特定的百分比。病例数最高的三个市镇是马瑙斯、塔巴廷加和圣保罗德奥利文萨。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者得出结论,防止亚马逊雨林原住民地区出现不受控制的虫媒病毒暴发需要健康 监测、文化尊重以及超越传统城市模式的领土保护。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为针对监测的、文化适宜的预防措施以及领土保护策略提供了信息,以降低土著社区的虫媒病毒风险。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 基于监测通报数据的回顾性描述性设计可能因报告不足和有限的人口统计学细节而证据强度中等。

papers.title: Phytochemical profiling, characterization, and antiviral evaluation of hydro alcoholic bark extract of Alstonia scholaris (L.) against DENV-2
papers.abstract: No antiviral drug or very few drugs are available to treat arboviral disease, dengue.The present study focuses on the design, extraction, and antiviral evaluation of hydroalcoholic bark extract of Alstonia scholaris linn.Hydroalcoholic extract of bark was prepared using Soxhlet apparatus.Phytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and steroids.UV-Visible spectroscopy exhibited characteristic absorption peaks at 200 nm, while FTIR analysis revealed functional groups corresponding to hydroxyl, carbonyl, and alkene groups, confirming the presence of stigmasterol.Quantitative HPTLC profiling using toluene: ethylacetate: formic acid (5:4:1) demonstrated an Rf value of 0.849 with a stigmasterol content of 0.2038 mg/100 mg extract.The cytotoxicity profile of the bark extract (BE) was determined on Vero CCL-81 cells using the MTT assay, showing a CC50 value 105.5 μg/mL at 120 h, indicating time-dependent cytotoxicity.Antiviral studies against Dengue virus serotype-2 (DENV-2) demonstrated moderate inhibitory activity during pre, co and post-treatment conditions.These findings suggest that hydroalcoholic bark extract possesses potential antiviral activity against DENV-2 and can serve as a promising natural source for further pharmacological exploration.
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the antiviral activity of hydroalcoholic bark extract of Alstonia scholaris against DENV-2, addressing the lack of effective antiviral drugs for dengue disease.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study designed and extracted hydroalcoholic bark extract of Alstonia scholaris and evaluated its antiviral activity against DENV-2 using Vero CCL-81 cells.
analysis.methods: The hydroalcoholic extract was prepared using a Soxhlet apparatus, and phytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and steroids. UV-Visible spectroscopy and FTIR analysis were used to identify functional groups, and HPTLC profiling quantified stigmasterol content. Cytotoxicity and antiviral studies were conducted using the MTT assay and pre, co, and post-treatment conditions.
analysis.main_results: The hydroalcoholic bark extract demonstrated moderate inhibitory activity against DENV-2 during pre, co, and post-treatment conditions. The CC50 value was 105.5 μg/mL at 120 h, indicating time-dependent cytotoxicity.

papers.title_zh: Alstonia scholaris (L.) 树皮水醇提取物的植物化学特征分析、表征及 抗病毒药物 评估针对 DENV-2
papers.source_body_en: No antiviral drug or very few drugs are available to treat arboviral disease, dengue.The present study focuses on the design, extraction, and antiviral evaluation of hydroalcoholic bark extract of Alstonia scholaris linn.Hydroalcoholic extract of bark was prepared using Soxhlet apparatus.Phytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, and steroids.UV-Visible spectroscopy exhibited characteristic absorption peaks at 200 nm, while FTIR analysis revealed functional groups corresponding to hydroxyl, carbonyl, and alkene groups, confirming the presence of stigmasterol.Quantitative HPTLC profiling using toluene: ethylacetate: formic acid (5:4:1) demonstrated an Rf value of 0.849 with a stigmasterol content of 0.2038 mg/100 mg extract.The cytotoxicity profile of the bark extract (BE) was determined on Vero CCL-81 cells using the MTT assay, showing a CC50 value 105.5 μg/mL at 120 h, indicating time-dependent cytotoxicity.Antiviral studies against Dengue virus serotype-2 (DENV-2) demonstrated moderate inhibitory activity during pre, co and post-treatment conditions.These findings suggest that hydroalcoholic bark extract possesses potential antiviral activity against DENV-2 and can serve as a promising natural source for further pharmacological exploration.
papers.abstract_zh: 目前几乎没有 抗病毒药物 药物或仅有极少药物可用于治疗虫媒病毒疾病——登革热。本研究聚焦于 Alstonia scholaris linn. 树皮水醇提取物的设计、提取及 抗病毒药物 评估。使用索氏提取器制备了树皮的水醇提取物。植物化学分析证实存在生物碱、苷类、黄酮类和类固醇。紫外-可见光谱在 200 nm 处显示特征吸收峰,FTIR 分析揭示了对应羟基、羰基和烯基的官能团,确认了存在豆甾醇。使用甲苯:乙酸乙酯:甲酸 (5:4:1) 的定量 HPTLC 分析显示 Rf 值为 0.849,豆甾醇含量为 0.2038 mg/100 mg 提取物。在 Vero CCL-81 细胞上使用 MTT 法测定树皮提取物 (BE) 的细胞毒性,显示 CC50 值为 105.5 μg/mL(120 h),表明其随时间增加的细胞毒性。针对 登革病毒 2 型 (DENV-2) 的 抗病毒药物 研究显示,在预处理、共处理和后处理 治疗 条件下具有中等抑制活性。这些结果提示水醇树皮提取物对 DENV-2 具有潜在的 抗病毒药物 活性,可作为进一步药理探索的有前景的天然来源。

papers.title: Zika virus produces two isoforms of the NS2A protein that play mutually exclusive roles in viral replication and virion assembly.
papers.abstract: Zika virus (ZIKV), dengue virus, and several other orthoflaviviruses cause disease outbreaks in human and animal populations worldwide. The orthoflaviviral nonstructural protein 2A (NS2A) is critical for both viral replication and virion assembly. However, due to its small size, hydrophobicity, and the absence of structural information or protein-specific antibodies, we lack a clear understanding of how NS2A participates in these disparate processes. Here, using endogenously tagged NS2A-containing viral RNAs, we reveal that two NS2A isoforms are present during ZIKV infection, including both full-length NS2A and a C-terminally truncated isoform, termed NS2Aα. Phylogenetic and conservation analyses combined with polyprotein cleavage assays suggest that both NS2A isoforms are generated via the viral protease and are conserved across the Orthoflavivirus genus. Finally, using assays for viral replication and infectious particle production, we demonstrate that the two distinct NS2A isoforms function at different stages of the viral life cycle, with full-length NS2A required for viral RNA replication and NS2Aα important for virion assembly. Taken together, our data helps shed light on the form(s) and function(s) of the NS2A protein and suggests that each NS2A isoform plays a mutually exclusive role in the orthoflaviviral life cycle.

papers.source_body_en: Zika virus (ZIKV), dengue virus, and several other orthoflaviviruses cause disease outbreaks in human and animal populations worldwide. The orthoflaviviral nonstructural protein 2A (NS2A) is critical for both viral replication and virion assembly. papers.abstract_zh: 寨卡病毒(ZIKV)、登革病毒以及几种其他正黄病毒科病毒在全球范围内引起疾病暴发。正黄病毒科的非结构蛋白2A(NS2A)对病毒复制和病毒颗粒组装至关重要。然而,由于其体积小、疏水性和缺乏结构信息或蛋白特异性抗体,我们对NS2A如何参与这些不同的过程仍缺乏清晰的理解。在此,我们利用内源性标记的NS2A含有病毒RNA,揭示了在ZIKV感染期间存在两种NS2A异构体,包括全长NS2A和一个C端截断的异构体,称为NS2Aα。系统发育和保守性分析结合多聚蛋白切割实验表明,这两种NS2A异构体均通过病毒蛋白酶生成,并在正黄病毒属中具有保守性。最后,通过病毒复制和感染性颗粒生成实验,我们证明这两种不同的NS2A异构体在病毒生命周期的不同阶段起作用,其中全长NS2A对于病毒RNA复制是必需的,而NS2Aα则在病毒颗粒组装中起重要作用。综上所述,我们的数据有助于阐明NS2A蛋白的形式和功能,并表明每种NS2A异构体在正黄病毒生命周期中发挥相互排斥的作用。

papers.title: Frequentist and Bayesian Interval Estimation for Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Incidence Rates with Application to Dengue Fever Surveillance
papers.abstract: A reliable interval estimation of the latent mean incidence rate is important but challenging in infectious disease surveillance because count data are often zero-inflated and overdispersed. This study compared frequentist (normal approximation (NA), bootstrap percentile (BP), and bootstrap-t (BT)) and Bayesian (equal-tailed interval (ETI) and highest density interval (HDI)) intervals under the zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model. A Monte Carlo simulation study varied levels of zero inflation, dispersion, and the observation period, evaluating conditional and unconditional coverage and average interval length. NA and BP showed undercoverage throughout the evaluated scenarios. BT improved conditional coverage over BP in 47 of 54 scenarios but generally produced wider intervals. Bayesian intervals often had higher coverage, although overcoverage and diagnostic failures prevented a uniform advantage. HDI was shorter than ETI in every scenario. An empirical application to dengue surveillance data from Phayao Province, Thailand, illustrated the five interval procedures under a fitted ZINB model; however, the NB model had lower AIC/BIC values. Temporal diagnostics and block bootstrap results indicated sensitivity to dependence assumptions. Overall, interval performance depended on the scenario, prior specification, and successful interval construction; no method uniformly achieved nominal coverage.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to improve interval estimation for zero-inflated and overdispersed incidence rates in dengue fever surveillance. It compared frequentist and Bayesian methods under a zero-inflated negative binomial model, using Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate coverage and interval length. The results showed that frequentist methods like NA and BP had undercoverage, while BT improved conditional coverage in most scenarios but resulted in wider intervals. Bayesian intervals generally had higher coverage, though overcoverage and diagnostic failures limited their uniform advantage. HDI was consistently shorter than ETI. The study highlights the importance of selecting appropriate interval estimation methods for dengue surveillance data, emphasizing that no single method uniformly achieves nominal coverage. These findings can inform more accurate surveillance practices and highlight the need for careful method selection based on data characteristics.

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究在零膨胀负二项分布(ZINB)模型下比较了频率学派(正态近似(NA)、百分位数Bootstrap(BP)和t Bootstrap(BT))和贝叶斯(等尾区间(ETI)和最高密度区间(HDI))区间估计方法。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过蒙特卡洛模拟研究,变化了零膨胀程度、离散程度和观察期长度,评估了条件覆盖和无条件覆盖以及平均区间长度。
analysis_zh.main_results: NA和BP在所有评估场景中均表现出覆盖不足。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: BT在54种情景中的47种情况下改善了条件覆盖,但通常产生更宽的区间。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 贝叶斯区间通常具有更高的覆盖,尽管过度覆盖和诊断失败阻止了其统一优势。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 在所有场景中,HDI都比ETI更短。

news.title: Florida Dengue Outbreak 2026: Symptoms, Testing, Treatment, and Prevention - Infection Control Today
news.rss_summary_html: Florida Dengue Outbreak 2026: Symptoms, Testing, Treatment, and Prevention  Infection Control Today
news.excerpt_original: Florida Dengue Outbreak 2026: Symptoms, Testing, Treatment, and Prevention Infection Control Today
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content: Trending on Infection Control Today Florida Dengue Outbreak 2026: Symptoms, Testing, Treatment, and Prevention Kenya’s Imported Ebola Case Raises Questions About Screening and IPC Readiness Shared Equipment, Missed Surfaces, and the Fight Against Antimicrobial Resistance How AI Supports Early Sepsis Detection in ICU and NICU Patients Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. In this podcast with ICT, Danielle Updegraff, MBA, BSN, RN, discusses real-time location systems, which can give infection prevention teams greater visibility into hand hygiene, workflow, and infectious disease exposures, but sustainable improvement still depends on staff engagement, leadership, education, and culture. In this complete interview, ICT speaks with Endale Tilahun, MD, MPH, about a Malawi community program that reduced missed HIV testing and achieved 0.2% positivity among exposed infants through household follow-up, individualized case management, and coordinated health and social support. Environmental testing found bacterial contamination on many lead garments and described what lead garment cleaning technicians routinely encounter during servicing. New research presented at AIDS 2026 indicates that 2-drug HIV regimens and long-acting injectable therapies are effective treatment options that also enhance personalized care. Investigators highlight that shared decision-making, adherence, quality of life, and minimizing long-term medication exposure are becoming more vital alongside maintaining viral suppression. International infection prevention leaders discuss how Ireland and Saudi Arabia educate, recruit, and prepare IPC professionals while advocating for broader, multidisciplinary career pathways worldwide. A hantavirus outbreak linked to a South American cruise ship is drawing global attention, but experts say fears of a COVID-19-style pandemic are largely unsupported. Infectious disease physician Matthew Pullen, MD, discusses Andes virus transmission, misinformation, cruise ship risks, and what health care professionals should really be watching for. The cohosts of Contagious Conversation speak with Tori Whitacre Martonicz, lead editor of Infection Control Today, about her presentation at the SoCal SPA Spring Conference, and how the conference speakers emphasized leadership beyond titles, urging SPD professionals to share knowledge, speak up, and turn everyday insights into safer patient care practices. Dental assistants manage sterilization, infection control, and patient education—yet most states require zero formal training. They earn the lowest wages in dental offices. Meet Sherrie Busby's 42-year mission to secure standardized credentialing and fair recognition. (Audio podcast) As her 2025 APIC presidency concludes, Carol McLay, DrPH, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, FSHEA, discusses public health funding cuts, science advocacy, global partnerships, workforce development, and why infection preventionists must speak up. In this exclusive ICT interview, she shares lessons from a tumultuous year and her vision for strengthening the infection prevention profession worldwide. An unexplained death at a Russian plague research institute has prompted international scrutiny. The incident raises questions about laboratory safety, transparent reporting, and infection prevention preparedness while the cause remains unconfirmed. Behind every landmark in infection prevention, from antimicrobial stewardship guidelines to the COVID-19 town halls that reached flight attendants and teachers, is a generation of physician-scientists who led SHEA through crises, organizational change, and scientific breakthroughs. Infection Control Today traces 30 years of SHEA presidents and the lasting mark they left on the field. Missing instruments and processing delays can strain OR–SPD relationships. At AORN 2026, John Kimsey, vice president of processing optimization and customer success for STERIS, discusses understanding root causes, exploring off-site reprocessing for ambulatory surgical centers, and using hands-on simulation to help surgical teams see sterile processing from a different perspective. This week's coverage in Infection Control Today centered on a common thread: the systems, partnerships, and data that let infection prevention teams catch problems before patients are harmed. UPMC’s genomic surveillance initiative earned national recognition for patient safety. Alexander Sundermann, DrPH, CIC, FAPIC, AL-CIP, explains how the award could help infection preventionists secure leadership support and sustainable funding for earlier outbreak detection. Knowing the protocol is only the beginning. In The Clean Bite, Sherrie Busby explores how explaining the why, addressing staff concerns, and creating clear procedures can help dental teams make infection control part of everyday practice. What might infection prevention rounds miss when visible conditions dominate the conversation? Tommy Davis, PhD, CMIP, a member of ICT's executive advisory board, makes the case for structured observations of clinical workflows, shared accountability, and greater attention to environmental services staff’s insights. A proposed $27.7 million reduction in AHRQ funding raises questions about support for infection prevention research and implementation. Here is what the September 25 announcement identifies, as well as what remains unknown about specific IPC programs. Two posters presented by Karen Jones, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, at the APIC Annual Conference and Exposition examine surveillance responsibilities and staffing in small hospitals, as well as IPs’ reported experiences after implementing electronic surveillance. Findings highlight opportunities for more investigation, rounding, and communication. A followed procedure can still leave patients at risk if it no longer matches validated requirements. Annetta L. news.content_zh: 来自《感染控制今日》的文章《佛罗里达登革热暴发 2026:症状、检测、治疗及预防》,于2026年10月12日发表,提供了关于登革病毒及其管理的概述。文章强调了在无菌处理和感染预防中应重视人为因素,指出需要加强员工参与、领导力和教育。文章还提到了医疗专业人员在保持安全和预防感染方面所面临的挑战。然而,该文章并未报告佛罗里达州有任何确诊病例、死亡或具体的暴发细节。相反,它是一篇关于登革热和感染控制实践的一般性讨论。文章提到,一位有发热症状且无近期旅行史的患者仍可能感染登革热,表明当地可能存在传播的可能性。文章未提供有关暴发规模或其对人口影响的数据。文章未详细说明响应状态,因为它主要关注更广泛的感染预防策略,而非针对登革热暴发的具体应对措施。

OffOn Stream on As dengue continues to rise in Florida, some are worried about underreporting of cases At least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in 6 counties. ByMary Kekatos September 30, 2026, 3:00 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google As cases of dengue fever continue to rise in Florida, public health specialists are worried the true number of infections may be greater. For the week ending Sept. 19, at least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue have been confirmed in the state, an increase of 38 cases from the week before, according to data from the Florida Department of Health (DOH). Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa, is reporting the highest number of cases at 170 followed by Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco and Pinellas counties, DOH data shows. Related What to know about dengue fever as Florida reports 1st death and cases rise "There's evidence of local transmission of dengue in several counties in Florida," Natalie Dean, an associate professor of biostatistics and informatics at Emory University's Rollins School of Public Health, told ABC News. "Dengue is not endemic to the United States. That means that it doesn't typically cause local transmission." She added, "There can be occasional outbreaks in the U.S. but this one is notable for its size." Last week, DOH reported the state's first death from dengue fever this year but did not provide any details about the patient including name, age, sex or residence. Close-up of a mosquito biting human skin. Joao Paulo Burini/Getty Images Three counties -- Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas -- declared local states of emergency last week. These allow local governments to waive normal procedures, access emergency resources and strengthen efforts to control mosquito populations. Pinellas County crews have been going door to door and spraying areas with high mosquito presence, according to local ABC News affiliate WFTS. "I don't recall a [period] of time when it's been this high in such a sort of concentrated area before," Cameron Wolfe, an infectious diseases specialist and a professor of medicine at Duke University School of Medicine, told ABC News. Wolfe said there may be an underestimate of the true number of cases in Florida. Cases of dengue can be mild, and people may recover on their own or never be tested. Because dengue can resemble a flu-like illness, patients may never suspect the source of their infection. Additionally, he said that reporting of confirmed cases to either local state departments or the CDC can lag. Popular Reads Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Oct 11 'Dancing with the Stars' season 35: See who is eliminated 21 hours ago Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia 1 day ago "For every case that we know, there's going to be a bunch that we never find out about," Wolfe said. Related Increased risk of dengue virus infections in the US: CDC Dean added that people can be infected with dengue multiple times over the course of their life, but it's usually the second or later infection that is more severe, leading to further underreporting. "I always think of like the top of an iceberg," Dean said. "We're only capturing some of the some of the cases." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) told ABC News in a statement on Tuesday that the agency is "closely tracking dengue activity" and the "unprecedented" number of cases in the Tampa area. The CDC also said they've provided $800,000 in emergency funds to help with the response. "Because the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, Aedes aegypti, are common throughout many areas of the United States, continued local spread of dengue is possible," the CDC statement said. "The best way to prevent dengue is to protect yourself from mosquito bites by using EPA-registered insect repellant, wearing loose fitting clothes, and controlling mosquitoes in and around your home, such as dumping water." Related Dengue fever cases rise to 6,800 in US amid 2 new infections in Los Angeles: CDC Some research has shown that climate change could be expanding the geographic range and severity of dengue fever. Rising global temperature coupled with more rainfall and humidity -- leading to standing water pools that serve as breeding grounds for mosquitoes -- could increase the number of cases. "Global warming and climate change, in fact, leave places like Florida more wet and more capable of housing these mosquito vectors, so I wouldn't be surprised if this becomes a little more of a perpetual thing," Wolfe said. analysis_en.time: As of the week ending Sept. 19, 2026, with the publication date being Oct.
analysis_en.location_and_population: Florida, United States, specifically in 6 counties, including Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Pinellas. At least 190 confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported.
analysis_en.event: Dengue cases continue to rise in Florida, with public health specialists expressing concerns about underreporting. The Florida Department of Health (DOH) confirmed at least 190 cases of locally acquired dengue in the state, an increase of 38 cases from the previous week. The first death from dengue fever this year was reported, though details about the patient were not provided.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: At least 190 confirmed cases of dengue in 6 counties, with Hillsborough County reporting the highest number at 170 cases. The CDC noted the "unprecedented" number of cases in the Tampa area and emphasized the potential for continued local spread due to the presence of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. There is a concern that the true number of infections may be higher due to underreporting and mild cases that may not be tested.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Three counties (Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas) declared local states of emergency, allowing for waived procedures and emergency resources to control mosquito populations. Local crews have been conducting door-to-door inspections and spraying high mosquito areas. The CDC has provided $800,000 in emergency funds and is closely tracking dengue activity. However, there are unresolved concerns about underreporting and the potential for further spread.

news.source_body_en: Dengue cases are rising in Florida, with at least 190 confirmed locally acquired infections reported in six counties as of the week ending Sept. 19, 2026. Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa, has the highest number of cases at 170. Public health specialists, including Natalie Dean from Emory University and Cameron Wolfe from Duke University, have raised concerns about underreporting, noting that many cases may go undetected due to mild symptoms or lack of testing. The CDC has acknowledged the "unprecedented" number of cases in the Tampa area and is closely monitoring the situation, having allocated $800,000 in emergency funds. Three counties—Hillsborough, Pasco, and Pinellas—have declared states of emergency to facilitate mosquito control efforts. Despite these measures, the risk of continued local transmission remains due to the presence of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and potential climate factors. The first death from dengue fever this year was reported, though details about the patient were not disclosed.

news.content: Florida Dengue Outbreak 2026: Symptoms, Testing, Treatment, and Prevention Florida’s dengue outbreak highlights the importance of recognizing symptoms, identifying warning signs, and preventing mosquito bites. Ubong Johnson, MD, explains local transmission, diagnostic testing, treatment, and practical prevention measures. Florida has recorded a recent spike in the number of dengue fever cases, with one death confirmed in September. The latest weekly update posted by the Florida Department of Health (Week 39, September 27 to October 3) confirms 296 locally acquired cases across 8 counties.1 Hillsborough County takes the biggest hit, with 259 cases and one confirmed death: an 80-year-old Tampa woman who died in September. Other affected counties are Pinellas (20), Miami-Dade (8), Orange (3), Pasco (3), Palm Beach (1), Polk (1), and Broward (1).1 The Florida dengue spike is likely due to international travel, an increase in local mosquito population, and low population immunity. These are plausible contributing factors; however, the surveillance report does not show that any one of them caused this outbreak. As an international travel hub, trade route, and center for tourism, Florida sees a continuous influx of visitors from endemic areas across Latin America and the Caribbean, some of whom are infected with the dengue virus.2 When Aedes aegypti, a mosquito species that prefers to feed in the daytime, or, less frequently, Aedes albopictus, bites a person with the dengue virus circulating in the blood, it can pick up the virus. This person may be an international visitor, a Florida resident returning from travel, or someone already infected locally, and may have no symptoms. When an infected mosquito bites someone else, it can spread the virus. There are 4 serotypes of dengue virus: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Of the local cases serotyped in the Week 39 report, 273 were DENV-2, and 2 were DENV-3. Because Aedes aegypti is a nervous mosquito that is easily disturbed while feeding, it will usually bite more than one person before completing a blood meal.3 More bites create more opportunities for transmission. As transmission bites and transmission continue, the dengue virus eventually enters the local population and starts to spread amongst locals without the need for international hosts.4 Heat contributes to the increasing rate of dengue fever transmission by increasing the local mosquito population and by shortening the extrinsic incubation period. The virus typically replicates in a mosquito’s midgut and spreads to other tissues, including the salivary gland, before transmission is possible. WHO says this takes about 8 to 12 days at 25–28°C. In hotter seasons, the virus can mature more quickly, leading to faster transmission.5 Since prior infection generally gives long-lasting protection against the same dengue virus serotype and only temporary protection against the other serotypes, people living in endemic areas usually develop a type of immunity against dengue fever called homotypic immunity.6 A second infection with a different dengue virus serotype can result in a more severe disease, as previously acquired antibodies act as “Trojan horses” that permit easier entry of the virus into the cell. Symptoms of dengue fever, if they appear, usually begin 4 to 6 days after the infecting bite. CDC’s yellow book describes a typical incubation of 5 to 7 days, within a range of about 3 to 10 days.7 Some people experience no symptoms. Where symptoms are present, dengue fever has 3 courses: a febrile phase, a critical phase, and a recovery phase.8 The febrile phase lasts 2 to 7 days and can occur in 2 phases. It begins with a high fever that reaches up to 104°F (40°C), a headache, and pain around the eyes. There may be muscle soreness, joint pain, fatigue, facial flushing, and loss of appetite.9 A rash usually shows up around 2 to 6 days after the fever starts, and there may be some bleeding trouble. In children and in patients who later develop a severe form of the disease, there may be signs of stomach trouble, such as nausea and vomiting. Most patients recover at the end of the febrile phase. The critical phase typically begins when the fever subsides and lasts 24 hours. About 1 in 20 people who become ill with dengue develop severe dengue.8 In severe dengue, fluid seeps out of blood vessels. This can cause fluid build-up around the lungs and in the abdomen, presenting as difficulty in breathing or abdominal swelling, respectively. Severe dengue is characterized by plasma leakage that causes shock or respiratory distress, severe bleeding, or severe organ involvement. Early compensated shock can occur before hypotension. A marked reduction in blood sodium can also occur, although this doesn’t define severe dengue. Some patients may experience bleeding due to a drop in platelet count, which shows up as blood in stool, blood in vomit, and excessive menstrual bleeding.10 As fluid leakage from blood vessels subsides, patients in the critical phase enter the recovery phase and begin to improve. Clinicians suspect dengue when a person has an acute fever and 2 or more classic symptoms, such as pain behind the eye, severe muscle ache, nausea/vomiting, or a maculopapular rash, especially if this person lives in or has recently traveled to an area with dengue transmission. Dengue fever is not confirmed clinically. Some lab work is needed to distinguish the disease from other conditions that resemble it, such as COVID-19, acute gastroenteritis, or leptospirosis. Testing helps confirm the diagnosis, but management of suspected dengue should begin without waiting for results. Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) detects dengue virus in serum and can identify the infecting serotype. Sensitivity depends on the assay, the specimen, and the timing. CDC recommends a nucleic acid test, such as RT-PCR, plus IgM or NS1 antigen plus IgM, during days 0 to 7 of illness. After day 7, IgM is the primary test. A negative RT-PCR or NS1 doesn’t rule out dengue.11 Dengue fever can be treated at home or in the hospital. At home, patients can benefit from drinking enough fluids, getting adequate rest, and taking acetaminophen for fever or pain. Aspirin and other NSAIDs, including ibuprofen, should be avoided because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Patients with warning signs, certain underlying health conditions, or an inability to keep down oral fluids may need hospital care. In the hospital, patients may be given IV fluids with careful monitoring to avoid fluid overload. Blood transfusion is considered when there is clinically significant bleeding or suspected occult bleeding. If you are currently experiencing any symptoms of dengue fever or know someone who is, seek medical care or encourage them to do so. Dengue fever is preventable.12 Prevention aims to break transmission cycles by stopping the vector from multiplying and biting people, as well as directly protecting individuals from the effects of a mosquito bite, should one get bitten. You can protect yourself from mosquito bites by using insect repellent, wearing loose-fitting long-sleeve clothes, using insecticide-treated nets, using air conditioners, and controlling mosquito populations around you. You can eliminate potential mosquito breeding grounds by emptying, covering, or cleaning containers that hold stagnant water. Public health agencies may support this by making larvicides available for use in non-potable water systems. Travel precautions can reduce the risk of the virus being introduced and spreading. CDC recommends that travelers returning from dengue-risk areas prevent mosquito bites for 3 weeks, even if they feel well, and watch out for symptoms for 2 weeks. There are currently no dengue vaccines available in the United States, under CDC guidance. Dengvaxia has been discontinued and is no longer available. And Qdenga is not available or recommended in the United States. Travelers should review destination-specific notes, receive pretravel advice, and prevent mosquito bites. supplementary_news.content_title: Florida dengue cases surge to 296, largest US outbreak in decades
supplementary_news.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Florida dengue cases surge to 296, largest US outbreak in decades State adds 44 more cases C. A. Bridges Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Oct. 9, 2026, 10:44 a.m. ET Florida has reported 296 locally acquired dengue fever cases this year, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The majority of cases, 259, have been confirmed in Hillsborough County, where one death has been reported. Several counties have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control, with 16 counties under a mosquito-borne illness alert or advisory. Florida reported 44 new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health. The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 296 for the year as of Oct. 3, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The bulk of the cases have been in Hillsborough County, which has 259 confirmed cases, while other locally acquired cases have been reported in seven other counties. Broward County reported its first confirmed human dengue case on Oct. 5. One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of “dengue infection” along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. Florida's surge began three months ago. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. Currently, 16 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. West Nile virus and chikungunya — which are also transmitted by mosquitoes — have also been reported in Florida this year, but in far fewer numbers than dengue. Another human case of West Nile was reported in Holmes County in the period of Sept. 27 - Oct. 3, bringing the state total to seven for the year. No new chikungunya cases were reported. ➤ Dengue cases keep climbing in Florida. This is how to protect yourself There have also been 262 dengue cases associated with international travel reported in Florida this year, 215 of which were from travel from Cuba, according to the FDOH. Most of the cases were reported in Miami-Dade County. Although these cases were not locally acquired, mosquitoes that bite infected people in the state can transmit the disease to others. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. Dengue still surging in Florida. See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 3, there have been 296 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 252 reported Oct. 1. There have also been seven positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. Dengue: 296 cases 259 in Hillsborough County 20 in Pinellas County 8 in Miami-Dade County 3 in Orange County 3 in Pasco County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 7 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 1 case 1 in Miami-Dade County What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? One reason for the surge in dengue cases is due to a comibation of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes. 16 mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Brevard Broward Holmes Leon Manatee Martin Palm Beach Polk Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Duval Hillsborough Miami-Dade Orange Pasco Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." All Florida residents could take precautions to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 10, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Dengue Transmission in Mexico Varies Sharply by Place, Year and Virus Serotype, Modelling Study Finds by October 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Dengue Transmission in Mexico Varies Sharply by Place, Year and Virus Serotype, Modelling Study Finds Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Dengue remains one of the most formidable mosquito-borne viral diseases in the Americas, and Mexico has stood at the front line of its recent resurgence. A new modelling study published in PLOS Medicine has now provided the most detailed picture to date of how intensely dengue virus has circulated across Mexico between 2016 and 2023, both overall and separately for each of the virus’s four serotypes. By analysing more than 833,000 probable or confirmed dengue cases reported to the country’s National Epidemiological Surveillance System, known as SINAVE, the research team quantified the force of infection, a measure of the rate at which susceptible individuals acquire infection, across 27 Mexican states. The results reveal striking spatial, temporal and serotype-specific heterogeneities that have important implications for how the country, and the wider region, plans vaccination strategies, vector control campaigns and outbreak preparedness. The study, led by Oliver S. Simmons and Ilaria Dorigatti together with colleagues at Mexican research institutions, set out to fill two important gaps in the understanding of dengue epidemiology. First, while earlier work had mapped long-term average spatial patterns of dengue risk in Mexico, nobody had systematically characterised how transmission intensity shifts from year to year across the country. Second, the relative transmissibility of the four dengue virus serotypes, DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4, remains poorly characterised both in Mexico and globally, despite the fact that these serotypes differ genetically and can dominate outbreaks at different times and places. Understanding these differences matters because infection with one serotype confers long-lasting immunity only against that serotype, while secondary infection with a different serotype is a well-established risk factor for severe disease. To address these questions, the researchers employed catalytic models, a class of mathematical models originally developed to describe age patterns of infection for vaccine-preventable diseases. These models use the age distribution of cases, combined with case counts over time, to estimate the force of infection without requiring population-wide serological surveys. Crucially, the team developed a new serotype-specific extension of these established models, allowing them to estimate how intensely each of the four serotypes was transmitting in each state and year. This methodological advance means that routinely collected case-notification data, which health ministries already gather as part of standard surveillance, can be repurposed to yield insights that would otherwise require expensive and logistically demanding seroprevalence studies. The analysis confirmed that dengue transmission in Mexico is far from uniform. Large spatial heterogeneities emerged, with some states experiencing consistently higher force of infection than others, reflecting differences in climate, urbanisation, mosquito abundance, human mobility and surveillance capacity. Equally notable were the temporal patterns: transmission intensity fluctuated considerably from year to year, underscoring that a single snapshot of average risk can be misleading for planning purposes. In years of intense transmission, a state’s population may experience a rapid accumulation of immunity, only for that same population to remain relatively untouched in subsequent years. This year-to-year volatility means that cumulative estimates of infection burden can conceal periods of both quiescence and explosive epidemic growth. The serotype-specific findings are among the most significant contributions of the study. DENV-1 and DENV-2, according to the model estimates, have historically circulated at high levels across Mexico, making them the dominant drivers of the country’s dengue burden during the study period. In contrast, DENV-4 exhibited low transmission intensity throughout the eight years analysed. Perhaps most concerning for public health planners was the evidence of increasing DENV-3 transmission intensity in several states in recent years, a trend that coincided with large outbreaks. Because many younger Mexicans may never have been exposed to DENV-3, its re-emergence creates a large susceptible population at risk of primary infection, while older cohorts previously exposed to this serotype decades ago face the possibility of secondary infection with a now-circulating different serotype, a scenario associated with elevated risk of severe dengue. The mechanistic underpinnings of these serotype-specific patterns are complex. Dengue virus transmission depends on the Aedes aegypti mosquito vector, whose abundance and susceptibility to infection can vary, as can the intrinsic fitness of each viral serotype. Differences in the force of infection between serotypes may reflect a combination of viral characteristics, such as replication efficiency in the mosquito and human host, and herd immunity dynamics, whereby a serotype that circulated widely in the past leaves fewer susceptible individuals available for future transmission. The modelling framework cannot fully disentangle these mechanisms on its own, but by generating comparable, state-level estimates of serotype-specific transmission intensity, it provides the empirical foundation upon which such mechanistic questions can be addressed in future work. The study also highlights the crucial role of diagnostics in making serotype-specific inference possible. Extensive reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, or RT-PCR, testing during the study period allowed many cases to be attributed to a specific infecting serotype, and the authors emphasise that newly available rapid diagnostic tests capable of discerning the infecting serotype could further improve this picture. As these tests become more widely deployed, surveillance systems in Mexico and elsewhere will be better positioned to track which serotypes are circulating in near real time, information that is directly relevant to decisions about when and where to deploy interventions. The timing is particularly significant given that Mexico has introduced dengue vaccination programmes, and vaccine effectiveness and deployment strategy can depend on the local transmission intensity and the serotype composition of circulating viruses. The authors are careful to note an important limitation: the serotype-specific estimates may be affected by heterogeneities in how cases are reported across states and over time. Surveillance intensity, health-seeking behaviour, access to healthcare and diagnostic practices all vary geographically and can shift between years, and disentangling genuine changes in transmission from artefacts of the reporting system remains a task for future validation studies. Nevertheless, the scale of the dataset, spanning 833,629 cases across 27 states and eight years, lends considerable weight to the broad patterns identified, and the consistency of the findings with known epidemiological events, such as the DENV-3 resurgence coinciding with large outbreaks, supports their plausibility. The wider context makes this work especially timely. Mexico and the Americas region as a whole have experienced rising dengue incidence in recent years, and there are widespread concerns that changing climatic conditions, including warmer temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns, may expand the geographic range and seasonal window of Aedes mosquito activity, thereby enhancing transmission in the future. In this environment, accurate estimates of who remains susceptible to which serotype, and where and when transmission is most intense, become essential inputs for targeting vaccination, vector control and clinical preparedness. The methods developed in this study contribute to a better understanding of the past and current burden of dengue infection and can help refine assessments of the potential impact of existing and new interventions, from next-generation vaccines to Wolbachia-based biocontrol strategies. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the power of mining routinely collected surveillance data with appropriately sophisticated models. Rather than relying solely on costly serological surveys, public health authorities can extract detailed, serotype-resolved pictures of transmission intensity from the case notifications they already gather, provided that diagnostic testing is sufficiently extensive and that reporting heterogeneities are acknowledged and, where possible, corrected for. As dengue continues to expand its footprint across the Americas under the combined pressures of urbanisation, connectivity and climate change, approaches of this kind offer a practical route toward the granular, timely evidence base that controlling this evolving threat will demand. supplementary_news.content_title: Florida dengue cases surge to 296, largest US outbreak in decades
supplementary_news.content: Florida reported 44 new locally acquired cases of dengue fever in one week, according to the latest update from the Florida Department of Health . The disease is also called breakbone fever, due to the pain it causes. That brings the statewide total to 296 for the year as of Oct. 3, the largest outbreak in the United States in decades. The previous highest number of Florida cases in recent memory was 199 in 2023 . In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases for the year. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The bulk of the cases have been in Hillsborough County, which has 259 confirmed cases, while other locally acquired cases have been reported in seven other counties. Broward County reported its first confirmed human dengue case on Oct. 5. One death was confirmed in Hillsborough County, identified as 80-year-old Gay Small, who died of "dengue infection" along with septic shock and multi-organ failure, according to a death certificate. The previous largest outbreak was in Hawaii's Big Island, where 264 local cases were reported in the six months between September 2015 and March 2016. Florida's surge began three months ago. ➤ Prevent dengue at home in Florida with this 10-minute mosquito inspection Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco , Hillsborough , and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. Currently, 16 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. West Nile virus and chikungunya — which are also transmitted by mosquitoes — have also been reported in Florida this year, but in far fewer numbers than dengue. Another human case of West Nile was reported in Holmes County in the period of Sept. 27 - Oct. 3, bringing the state total to seven for the year. No new chikungunya cases were reported. ➤ Dengue cases keep climbing in Florida. This is how to protect yourself There have also been 262 dengue cases associated with international travel reported in Florida this year, 215 of which were from travel from Cuba, according to the FDOH. Most of the cases were reported in Miami-Dade County. Although these cases were not locally acquired, mosquitoes that bite infected people in the state can transmit the disease to others. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites, including advice from the Florida Department of Health. According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Oct. 3, there have been 296 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported in seven counties, which is up from 252 reported Oct. 1. There have also been seven positive samples of West Nile virus and one case of chikungunya. 2 in Duval County (1 an asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) One reason for the surge in dengue cases is due to a comibation of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes . A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." "Residents throughout the state should continue to take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying bug spray, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitos are most active," said Isabella White, FDOH press secretary via email Sept. 23. White said FDOH "continues to coordinate with local mosquito control partners to support surveillance and targeted response efforts in affected areas. These efforts help reduce mosquito populations, limit the risk of disease transmission, and protect residents across Florida." " Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname "breakbone fever") Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue is sometimes called " breakbone fever " because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight, or premature birth. "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body's immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don't accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. C.A. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever cases are on the rise in Hanoi, raising concerns about a potential outbreak. Experts warn that dengue fever patients can develop severe symptoms within just a few days, especially if they are complacent after the fever subsides or self-medicate without a doctor's prescription. Báo Đầu tư•14/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 According to the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from October 2nd to the present, the city has recorded 400 cases of dengue fever in 81 wards and communes. This week, the city recorded 12 new outbreaks, bringing the cumulative total from the beginning of the year to 4,351 cases in 120 wards and communes with 193 outbreaks. Currently, 27 outbreaks remain active. Although the number of cases since the beginning of the year is lower than the average for the 2021-2025 period, data from this week shows that the disease is still circulating in the city. Notably, the period from September to November each year is when Hanoi intensifies surveillance and implements dengue fever prevention and control measures. Currently, dengue fever vaccines are available in Vietnam, adding another preventive measure alongside mosquito control. Many dengue fever patients are hospitalized with thrombocytopenia, bleeding, and liver damage. Doctors warn that from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, even if the fever has subsided, patients are still at risk of developing severe symptoms, including dengue shock, if not monitored and treated promptly. Recently, the number of dengue fever cases in Gia Lam commune and surrounding areas has been on the rise. At the Infectious Diseases Department of Gia Lam General Hospital, many patients are admitted with symptoms such as thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, bleeding, and other disorders requiring close monitoring. Some cases have developed serious complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, hypotension, elevated liver enzymes, and liver damage. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, Head of the Infectious Diseases Department at Gia Lam General Hospital, what is worrying is that many people still consider dengue fever to be just a common fever. In the early days, when symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and body aches appear, many people self-medicate at home, believing it to be just the flu or a fever due to a change in weather. Only when abdominal pain, vomiting, extreme fatigue, or unusual bleeding occurs do patients seek medical attention. Meanwhile, dengue fever can progress very rapidly. Some patients may be alert and able to eat in the early days, but then suddenly show warning signs of worsening condition, requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment. Notably, the period from the 3rd to the 7th day after the onset of fever is usually the time when patients need to be especially vigilant. This is the period when increased vascular permeability, plasma leakage, blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and other dangerous complications may occur. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, one common mistake is that patients assume they have recovered and stop monitoring their condition because their body temperature has decreased and their fever has subsided. In reality, the fever-reducing phase may coincide with the onset of warning signs of severe dengue fever. Symptoms that require special attention include severe or progressively worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, extreme fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, vomiting blood, black stools, or unusual vaginal bleeding. Decreased urination, cold hands and feet, and cold, clammy skin may also indicate circulatory disorders and a risk of shock. Doctors advise that patients should not wait until all symptoms appear before going to the hospital. As soon as there are warning signs or unusual changes in health, patients should seek immediate medical attention to assess the severity of the illness and receive timely intervention. At the Infectious Diseases Department of Gia Lam General Hospital, doctors treated patient D.D.A., who had dengue fever with thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). The patient was admitted for monitoring, underwent necessary tests, and was prescribed platelet transfusions based on clinical assessment. After the infusion, the patient continued to be monitored for signs of bleeding and laboratory test results. Throughout the treatment process, the patient's health condition improved. Based on this case, Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu noted that thrombocytopenia is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but not every case of thrombocytopenia requires platelet transfusion. The decision to transfuse must be based on the clinical condition, the degree of thrombocytopenia, bleeding manifestations, and related risk factors. Platelet transfusions are not routinely performed solely to increase platelet count. Patients should adhere to their doctor's assessment and instructions, and avoid attempting to increase platelet count using unproven methods. For dengue fever cases where doctors recommend home monitoring, patients need rest, adequate hydration, and may use oral rehydration solutions as directed. They should also closely monitor their health. Family members should assist in observing the patient's alertness, fluid intake, frequency of urination, abdominal pain, vomiting, and any signs of unusual bleeding. You may also like In symptomatic treatment, patients can use paracetamol to reduce fever as directed by healthcare professionals. Absolutely do not self-administer aspirin or ibuprofen due to the risk of increased bleeding. Self-administering intravenous fluids at home also carries many risks if not properly assessed and prescribed. Doctors emphasize that not all dengue fever cases require hospitalization. However, the decision to monitor at home must be based on professional assessment, and patients need clear instructions on when to return for follow-up appointments and what signs require immediate hospitalization. Besides early detection and timely treatment, prevention remains crucial in the context of a rising number of cases. According to Dr. Ngo Trong Hieu, the core measure is controlling disease-carrying mosquitoes, eliminating breeding grounds for larvae and pupae, and reducing the risk of mosquito bites. Residents should regularly inspect their living areas, collecting bottles, plastic containers, old tires, and other items that can collect water. Household water containers must be tightly covered and cleaned regularly. Additionally, each family should maintain the habit of sleeping under mosquito nets, even during the day, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and using appropriate mosquito control measures. In particular, families with a member infected with dengue fever need to take extra precautions against mosquito bites to protect the patient and reduce the risk of mosquitoes sucking blood from infected individuals and then transmitting the disease to others. Currently, dengue fever vaccines are available in Vietnam, adding another preventive measure alongside mosquito control. People can visit vaccination centers for advice on age, eligibility, and appropriate vaccination schedules. Experts advise that dengue fever can be effectively monitored and treated if detected early, the severity of the disease is accurately assessed, and professional guidelines are followed. However, people should not be complacent about changes in their bodies, especially during the period from the 3rd to the 7th day. The disappearance of fever does not mean the dangerous phase is over. Proactively seeking medical attention, closely monitoring warning signs, and promptly going to a healthcare facility are crucial factors in minimizing the risk of shock, severe bleeding, and life-threatening complications. In addition, many people make mistakes in using medication during dengue fever treatment. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung, senior professional advisor of Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination System, said that paracetamol (acetaminophen) is used to reduce fever in dengue fever cases. Meanwhile, patients should not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as diclofenac or naproxen. It's worth noting that these are all fairly common medications, often thought of by people when experiencing fever, headache, or body aches. Dengue fever can cause thrombocytopenia and blood clotting disorders. In this context, the effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) on platelet function may increase the risk of bleeding. Aspirin causes irreversible inhibition of platelet aggregation, while other NSAIDs can also reduce platelet aggregation to varying degrees. This group of drugs can also damage the gastric and duodenal mucosa, thereby increasing the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Another risk relates to kidney function. People with dengue fever may experience reduced circulating volume due to plasma leakage. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis in the kidneys, which can decrease renal blood flow and increase the risk of acute kidney injury. Furthermore, the strong pain-relieving effects of the medication may partially mask symptoms, making it more difficult to recognize warning signs of worsening illness. For adults weighing over 50 kg, paracetamol is typically administered at a dose of 500-1000 mg per dose, every 4-6 hours as needed, with a total dose not exceeding 4000 mg in 24 hours. However, the total amount of paracetamol must be calculated from all medications the patient is currently taking. Individuals with liver disease, kidney disease, frequent alcohol use, or malnutrition (weighing less than 50 kg) should exercise particular caution. Dosage and dosing intervals may need adjustment depending on individual circumstances and should be guided by a healthcare professional. You may also like A common situation is that patients have taken ibuprofen or aspirin before knowing they have or suspect they have dengue fever. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung advises patients not to panic and to absolutely not to self-medicate to "counteract" the medication they have taken. The necessary action is to stop taking aspirin, ibuprofen, and other NSAIDs, then inform the doctor specifically about the name of the medication, dosage, time of use, and number of doses taken so that an appropriate assessment can be made. If fever reduction or pain relief is needed, patients can use paracetamol at an appropriate dose. More importantly, their health condition should continue to be closely monitored to promptly detect any abnormal signs. Another risk comes from combination cold and flu medications. Many products already contain paracetamol, but users don't pay attention to the ingredient and then take additional paracetamol separately to reduce fever. Combining the doses from multiple products can lead to an overdose. Some cold and flu medications may contain ibuprofen, aspirin, or other ingredients unsuitable for people suspected of having dengue fever. Therefore, experts advise against self-medicating with combination cold and flu medications during this period. Besides using the correct medication, one development in dengue fever that patients often overlook is the reduction or disappearance of fever. Associate Professor, Doctor of Pharmacy Nguyen Tuan Dung notes that the disappearance of fever does not mean recovery. When body temperature returns to normal, patients can stop taking fever-reducing medication but must continue to monitor their health. The critical phase of the illness can occur around the 3rd to 8th day after infection, especially around the time the patient's fever subsides. Several serious complications can develop during this period and progress within 24-48 hours. Patients should seek immediate medical attention if they experience any unusual symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nosebleeds, vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, rapid breathing, lethargy, restlessness, cold hands and feet, or decreased urination.
