Some children carry the virus with barely a symptom, while others with the same infection progress to hospitalization with severe plasma leakage and shock. A new study of Cambodian children infected with dengue virus suggests that part of the answer lies not in how much antibody the immune system produces, but in the quality and specificity of the antibody-secreting cells mobilized during the acute phase of infection. The research, published in PLOS Pathogens, was led by Amandine Trouchet and colleagues working across institutes in France and Cambodia, including teams at the Institut Pasteur and the Institut Pasteur du Cambodge. The investigators set out to examine a question that has long frustrated dengue immunologists: which antibody features actually mediate protection in humans? Although dengue vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies have been developed, the correlates of protection against severe disease remain poorly defined, in large part because the human antibody response to dengue is exceptionally complex. That complexity stems from the structure of the virus itself. Dengue virus is coated with 180 copies of the envelope protein, known simply as E, which is the principal target of neutralizing antibodies. On the mature virion surface, E proteins are arranged as 90 homodimers, and this dimeric arrangement creates quaternary epitopes—antigenic surfaces that exist only when two E proteins are paired together. Antibodies that recognize these quaternary epitopes tend to be highly neutralizing and broadly reactive across the four dengue virus serotypes, whereas antibodies that bind only to isolated E monomers are frequently weakly neutralizing or even non-neutralizing, and in some contexts can contribute to antibody-dependent enhancement, the phenomenon in which pre-existing antibodies facilitate infection of cells by a different serotype. To dissect the antibody response at the level of individual cells, the team turned to droplet-based microfluidics, a technology that allows thousands of single antibody-secreting cells to be captured and analyzed in parallel. Each cell is enclosed in its own microscopic droplet together with fluorescently labeled viral antigens, so that the antibodies secreted by that single cell can be imaged as they bind to the antigen in real time. Using this approach, the researchers profiled more than 3,300 individual IgG-secreting cells from pediatric patients enrolled in a Cambodian cohort, comparing children with subclinical dengue infections against those who were hospitalized with symptomatic disease. The cohort was carefully structured to allow meaningful comparisons. The children had experienced either acute DENV1 or DENV2 infection, and the analysis focused on post-primary infections, meaning the patients were responding to dengue for at least the second time. This distinction matters because primary and secondary dengue infections generate qualitatively different antibody repertoires, and secondary infections carry a substantially higher risk of severe outcomes, a pattern thought to be driven in part by cross-reactive but poorly neutralizing antibodies generated during the first encounter with the virus. The first major finding was quantitative. Hospitalized patients had significantly fewer IgG-secreting cells in their circulation than children with subclinical infections, despite the fact that the cells they did possess secreted IgG at comparable rates. Moreover, when the researchers calculated the frequency of dengue E-specific antibody-secreting cells as a proportion of the total IgG-secreting population, they found no significant difference between the two groups. In other words, the immune systems of hospitalized children were not failing to target dengue specifically; they were simply mounting a smaller overall antibody-secreting response, leaving fewer antigen-specific cells available to fight the infection. The second finding concerned antibody affinity, a measure of how tightly an antibody binds its target. When the secreted antibodies from single cells were tested against the DENV1 envelope dimer, the antibodies from hospitalized patients showed a threefold lower average affinity than those from subclinical cases. Affinity matters enormously in antiviral defense: high-affinity antibodies neutralize virus more efficiently, persist longer in memory, and are more likely to mediate protective Fc-dependent functions. A threefold reduction across a population of antibody-secreting cells suggests that the germinal center reaction—the specialized structure in lymphoid tissue where B cells refine their antibodies through mutation and selection—was less effective in the children who went on to develop severe disease. The most striking qualitative difference emerged when the researchers probed the specificity of the antibodies for quaternary epitopes. Because quaternary epitopes depend on the dimeric arrangement of E on the virion, antibodies that bind the E dimer but not the E monomer are considered quaternary-epitope-specific. When the team compared binding to dimeric versus monomeric E protein, they found that antibodies recognizing quaternary epitopes were detected exclusively in the subclinical group. Hospitalized patients, by contrast, predominantly produced monomer-reactive antibodies—antibodies that bind the envelope protein in isolation and therefore, by inference, are less likely to recognize the authentic viral surface with the precision required for potent neutralization. Taken together, these results sketch a coherent picture of what distinguishes a protective dengue antibody response from a failing one. Children who weathered infection without hospitalization generated larger numbers of antibody-secreting cells, with higher average affinity for the envelope dimer and a clear representation of quaternary-epitope-specific clones. Hospitalized children produced fewer cells, of lower affinity, skewed toward monomer reactivity. The authors propose that dengue severity may be linked to the inefficient generation of sufficient numbers of high-affinity, broadly reactive antigen-specific IgG-secreting cells during post-primary infection, rather than to any single deficit in antibody quantity alone. The study carries implications for vaccine design and for the long-standing effort to define immune correlates of protection against dengue. Vaccines that reliably elicit quaternary-epitope-specific, high-affinity antibodies—rather than merely high titers of cross-reactive monomer-binding antibodies—may better recapitulate the response pattern associated with subclinical outcomes. The single-cell microfluidic approach also offers a template for future studies, since it captures the true diversity of the antibody-secreting cell population rather than averaging signals across bulk serum. As the authors note, the antibody features that mediate protection in humans remain poorly defined, and this work in a well-characterized Cambodian pediatric cohort provides some of the clearest evidence yet that the monoclonal composition of the early antibody response, not just its magnitude, shapes the clinical trajectory of dengue virus infection. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Temukan lebih banyak Berita Politik Cari Referensi Berita Gaya Hidup Home Health Hawaii Confirms Ninth Travel Related Dengue Case in 2026 Hawaii Confirms Ninth Travel Related Dengue Case in 2026 Ashley Morgan Published Oct 15, 2026 - 01:30 2 Reads Last Update Oct 15, 2026 - 01:30 Share WhatsApp Joe Raedle | Getty Images Smallest Font Largest Font Hawaii health officials have confirmed a ninth dengue case in the state in 2026 after a traveler became infected while visiting a region where the virus is common. Announced on October 13 and 14, the case was identified on Oahu, prompting inspections and mosquito control measures as authorities work to limit local transmission following recent heavy rainfall. The Hawaii Department of Health said the new infection has no known connection to previously reported cases. All nine dengue cases recorded in Hawaii this year involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories, and officials said the disease has not become established in the state. Health department teams have been dispatched to the affected area to identify mosquito breeding sites and implement control measures. Although mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue live in Hawaii, officials consider the current risk of local transmission low. The department is urging residents to remove standing water from outdoor containers, including buckets, planters, rain barrels, cups and water-catching plants. Recent rainfall can create additional breeding sites, allowing mosquito populations to grow around homes and workplaces. Dengue spreads when a mosquito bites an infected person and subsequently transmits the virus by biting another person. Symptoms can include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches, generally lasting two to seven days. Most patients recover within a week, although severe illness is possible. The department recommends that travelers visiting affected regions use an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants, and sleep in air-conditioned or screened rooms or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas where dengue occurs should continue preventing mosquito bites for three weeks. According to the department's guidance, people who develop symptoms within two weeks of returning from an affected area should seek medical evaluation. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection can contact the Hawaii Department of Health's Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. Florida is facing a separate and more extensive outbreak of locally acquired dengue infections. A Florida surveillance report covering cases through October 3 recorded 296 locally acquired cases statewide, including 259 in Hillsborough County, according to MedicalDaily. The county had increased aerial and ground mosquito treatments as officials assessed whether to extend its local emergency declaration, which was scheduled to expire October 15. Hillsborough County's mosquito control operations include daytime helicopter applications of Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, or Bti, to standing water to target mosquito larvae. An October 11 report from Osprey Observer said treatments were planned from October 12 through October 16 in Bloomingdale, Palm River, East Tampa and East Lake, where mosquito surveillance had indicated dengue virus activity. Florida Department of Health officials in Hillsborough County have emphasized that mosquito treatments alone cannot eliminate the risk. Removing water-holding containers remains an important part of prevention because mosquitoes that transmit dengue can breed in small amounts of standing water. Public health leaders in Karnataka, India, have also called for continuous dengue prevention rather than relying primarily on seasonal outbreak responses. A multi-stakeholder meeting in Bengaluru brought together government representatives, researchers, public health institutions and civil society organizations to develop a four-point action plan. Karnataka Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader Fareed said the recent decline in cases should not lead to complacency. He called for stronger surveillance, diagnostics, mosquito monitoring, vaccination research and community-based prevention as environmental conditions continue to influence transmission. School Education and Literacy Minister Madhu Bangarappa highlighted the role of schools in public awareness and prevention. Participants proposed year-round education, stronger links between community screening and healthcare, coordinated state and municipal surveillance data, and investment in locally adapted technology for mosquito monitoring. FOX 51 Gainesville Tampa News - FOX 13 News Atlanta News - FOX 5 Atlanta FOX Weather About Us How to stream FOX 35 FOX 35 TV Schedule Contact Us Meet the team Work for Us FOX 35 Internships Sign up for FOX 35 emails Download FOX 35 apps Advertise with Us WRBW/FOX Orlando + Closed Captioning FCC Public File FCC Applications News Tips Call: (407) 741-5027 Email: FOX35News@FOX.com Share videos and photos with FOX 35 FOX 35 Connect Contests Stream on FOX One NFL Live Streaming College Football Live Streaming MLB Live Streaming NASCAR Live Stream IndyCar Live Streaming Men's College Basketball Live Stream Women's College Basketball Live Stream WNBA Live Stream MLS Live Stream River Flood Warning is in effect, Lake County, Volusia County Dengue fever: 2 more cases reported in Orange County, bringing total to 5, officials say By Josh Frigerio Apopka Published October 12, 2026 4:58 PM EDT Published October 12, 2026 4:58 PM EDT article The Brief Two more cases of locally-acquired dengue fever have been reported in Orange County, health officials said. That brings the total number of cases in Orange County this year to 5. Orange County Mosquito Control plans to spray for mosquitos in Apopka and Pine Hills over the next two weeks. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - Two more cases of locally-acquired dengue fever have been reported in Orange County, according to the Florida Department of Health, bringing the total number of cases this year to five. Orange County officials plan to conduct more sprays targeting mosquitos known to transmit dengue fever. Dengue fever cases in Orange County. Here's where. By the numbers: According to the Florida Department of Health and Orange County Mosquito Control, the five cases have been reported in Pine Hills and Apopka: Sept. 1: 1 confirmed case in Pine Hills area Sept. 18: 2 confirmed cases in the Apopka area Oct. 12: 2 more confirmed cases in the Apopka area What we don't know: Officials have not released specifics about the persons who've contracted the virus, nor updates on their conditions. What is dengue fever? Why you should care: Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Signs and symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Florida Department of Health: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea There is no treatment for dengue fever. However, the CDC recommends people treat their symptoms early to manage potential complications. Orange County to spray for mosquitoes Timeline: Orange County Mosquito Control said it plans to conduct aerial spraying in Apopka and Pine Hills over the next several weeks to target mosquito populations known to transmit Dengue Fever. When will those sprays happen? Officials said residents will be notified at least 48 hours in advance via the county's social media channels, website, and through OC Alert notification. Click here to sign up to receive an alert. Tips to avoid mosquito bites What you can do: "It is very important for residents to ensure that there is no standing water on their property. We encourage residents to walk around their yards after a storm and drain any standing water, toss out anything that could hold water, and protect yourself with long sleeves, pants, and EPA-approved mosquito repellent," said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control in a statement. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed More on dengue fever Dig deeper: CDC: Dengue fever FDOH: Dengue fever in Florida Florida weekly arbovirus surveillance report Orange County Mosquito Control The Source: This story uses information gathered from the Florida Department of Health in Orange County (FDOH), Orange County Mosquito Control, the Florida Department of Health's Arbovirus Surveillance report, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and previous reporting by FOX 35. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Hanoi records 400 dengue fever cases in one week: Warning signs that cannot be ignored. GĐXH - Experts warn that dengue fever patients can experience severe symptoms within just a few days, especially if they are complacent after the fever subsides or self-medicate without a doctor's prescription. Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•13/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever is on the rise, and many people easily mistake it for a common fever. According to the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from October 2nd to October 9th, 2026, the city recorded 400 cases of dengue fever across 81 wards and communes. During the week, the city recorded 12 new outbreaks. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to date, Hanoi has had 4,351 cases in 120 wards and communes with 193 outbreaks. Currently, 27 outbreaks remain active. Dengue fever is on the rise, and many people easily mistake it for a common fever. (Illustrative image.) Although the number of cases since the beginning of the year is lower than the average for the 2021-2025 period, data from this week shows that the disease is still circulating in the city. Notably, the period from September to November each year is when Hanoi intensifies surveillance and implements dengue fever prevention and control measures. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA According to experts, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Initial symptoms usually include a sudden high fever, headache, eye pain, muscle and joint aches, possibly accompanied by nausea or a rash. These symptoms are easily mistaken for other viral fevers, leading patients to self-medicate or delay seeking medical attention. In fact, over the past period, many hospitals in Hanoi have received and treated numerous cases of dengue fever with complicated symptoms. In September 2026 alone, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases reported that it had received and treated dengue fever cases with diverse manifestations, including many severe cases. Notably, a 37-year-old female patient initially thought she only had a common cold and self-medicated with fever-reducing drugs, but to no avail. On the second day of her illness, she developed severe headaches, high fever, and bleeding gums, and was subsequently diagnosed with Dengue fever. According to Dr. Nguyen Thanh Binh, Deputy Head of the Virology - Parasitology Department at the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases, people often make several mistakes when contracting dengue fever, leading to delays in detection and monitoring. One common mistake is self-medicating when fever and headache first appear. In particular, before ruling out dengue fever, patients should not self-medicate with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), as these drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Lowering the fever does not mean the danger is over. You may also like According to Dr. Binh, from the 3rd to the 7th day of dengue fever, especially when the patient's fever begins to subside or disappear, some cases may enter a dangerous phase. At this time, increased vascular permeability can lead to plasma leakage; in severe cases, it can cause decreased circulating volume, hypotension, and shock. Platelets may also decrease, and the patient may exhibit hemorrhagic symptoms. Doctors advise people not to be complacent when contracting dengue fever. Photo: National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Meanwhile, when body temperature returns to near normal, many people become complacent, assuming the illness is cured and neglecting monitoring. In reality, this is a stage that requires close monitoring to promptly detect any warning signs. Therefore, if diagnosed with dengue fever and being monitored at home, patients need to adhere to their scheduled follow-up appointments, monitor for any unusual symptoms, and follow the instructions of healthcare professionals. Do not discontinue monitoring simply because your body temperature has returned to normal. The elderly , young children, pregnant women, and people with underlying conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, kidney disease, or those undergoing cancer treatment require special attention. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, these individuals should seek medical attention early so that a doctor can assess the risk and provide appropriate monitoring guidance. For fever-reducing medication, patients should only use it as directed by a healthcare professional. Do not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as this may increase the risk of bleeding. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics, herbal remedies, or products of unknown ingredients. Currently, there is no specific, routinely used treatment for dengue fever to eliminate the dengue virus. Care and treatment mainly focus on close monitoring, symptom management, and timely intervention in case of complications. Patients should not self-administer intravenous fluids at home, as inappropriate fluid replacement can be dangerous. In particular, when symptoms such as persistent high fever, severe abdominal pain (especially in the liver and epigastric region), frequent vomiting, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vomiting blood, black stools, irregular menstruation, extreme fatigue, lethargy, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, or any other unusual symptoms appear, patients should immediately go to a medical facility for timely assessment and treatment to avoid possible complications. Actively eliminate mosquitoes and destroy breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. You may also like According to experts, alongside early detection of disease symptoms, preventing mosquito bites and eliminating breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes are crucial measures to limit the transmission of dengue fever. People should cover water containers tightly, regularly clean jars, pots, buckets, and basins; change the water in flower vases, remove stagnant water from trays, old tires, and other items around the house. They should sleep under mosquito nets, wear long-sleeved clothing, use appropriate mosquito repellents, and cooperate with local authorities in environmental sanitation, mosquito larva eradication, and chemical spraying when instructed. In addition, people can proactively learn about and get vaccinated against dengue fever according to appropriate guidelines and indications. With dengue fever cases still being recorded in many wards and communes in Hanoi, experts advise that each family should proactively take preventive measures and not be complacent when symptoms such as fever appear. Early recognition of warning signs, timely medical examination, and adherence to treatment guidelines are crucial factors in limiting the risk of severe complications from dengue fever. Article will play after ad... Playing in :00 A A A Kaua‘i mosquito trapping (Aug. 25, 2022). PC: Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources The Hawai‘i Department of Health reports identifying a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases in the state to eight for 2026. All of the cases have involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories. The affected individual was exposed to the virus while traveling in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi have been found. Health department teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito control measures in the affected area. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent heavy rain, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the Vector Control Branch website. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bangladesh, Bolivia, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Kenya, Malaysia, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Panama, Sri Lanka, Vanuatu and Vietnam. Travelers should review current, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, as well as sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, Health Department vector control personnel conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease are on the rise, raising concerns about life-threatening complications. In just one week, Ho Chi Minh City recorded more than 3,100 cases of dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease, with the number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases increasing by nearly 48%. Báo Đầu tư•09/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 The infectious disease situation in Ho Chi Minh City continues to be complex, especially with dengue fever and hand, foot, and mouth disease, two diseases that can spread rapidly and cause dangerous complications if not detected and treated promptly. Worryingly, the number of hand, foot, and mouth disease cases is increasing sharply, while dengue fever remains at a high level, increasing pressure on disease prevention and control efforts. According to data from the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), in week 40, from September 28 to October 4, 2026, the city recorded 1,505 cases of dengue fever, a decrease of 2.3% compared to the average of the previous four weeks. Despite the slight downward trend, the number of cases remains concerning, bringing the total number of dengue fever cases from the beginning of the year to the end of week 40 to 37,369. Health experts emphasize that proactive disease prevention is of particular importance, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. Localities with high dengue fever incidence rates per 100,000 people include Con Dao Special Zone, Ngai Giao, and Minh Thanh. These areas require continued strengthening of epidemiological surveillance, control of disease-carrying mosquitoes, and handling of outbreaks to limit the risk of community spread. Meanwhile, hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) has seen an alarming increase. In week 40 alone, the city recorded 1,673 cases, a 47.8% increase compared to the average of the previous four weeks. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to the end of week 40, Ho Chi Minh City has recorded 38,463 cases of HFMD. Areas with high incidence rates include Con Dao Special Economic Zone, Binh Khanh, and Hiep Phuoc. Thus, in just one week, these two infectious diseases have infected 3,178 people. These figures show that the risk of an epidemic still exists, especially in the context of unpredictable weather and the group learning and living activities of young children, which create conditions for disease-causing agents to spread. The worrying aspect lies not only in the number of cases but also in the risk of severe complications, even death, associated with both diseases. Dengue fever can progress rapidly from initial symptoms such as high fever, headache, and body aches to plasma leakage, shock, severe bleeding, and multi-organ failure. In particular, the dangerous phase of dengue fever usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, when the patient's fever may subside or disappear. The misconception that the absence of fever means recovery can cause patients to miss warning signs, increasing the risk of serious complications. For hand, foot, and mouth disease, most cases resolve spontaneously, but some cases, especially in young children, can progress to severe complications such as neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory problems. Symptoms such as persistently high fever, startled reactions, tremors, unsteady gait, abnormal breathing, or lethargy are warning signs that require urgent medical attention and treatment. You may also like In fact, the danger of hand, foot, and mouth disease also lies in its rapid progression, with some cases becoming severe in a short time. Children with the disease who are not closely monitored may develop life-threatening complications, especially in cases involving highly virulent enterovirus strains such as EV71. Given this situation, health experts emphasize that proactive disease prevention is of paramount importance, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. For dengue fever, Vietnam uses the Qdenga vaccine. This vaccine is administered to children aged 4 years and older and adults, including those who have previously had the disease, and helps prevent all four types of dengue virus. The vaccination schedule consists of two doses, administered three months apart. The protective efficacy is over 80%, reducing the risk of hospitalization due to dengue fever by over 90% when the full vaccination regimen is completed. Experts believe the greatest significance of the vaccine lies not only in reducing the risk of contracting the disease but also in limiting severe cases, easing the burden on the healthcare system during outbreaks, and contributing to the protection of high-risk groups such as children. However, the vaccine is not suitable for people who are hypersensitive to any of its components, pregnant women, or breastfeeding mothers. For immunocompromised individuals or those with HIV, please consult a healthcare professional for guidance tailored to your specific situation. Regarding hand, foot, and mouth disease, a notable point is that the Ministry of Health has approved a vaccine against hand, foot, and mouth disease caused by the EV71 virus, opening up opportunities to prevent severe complications of the disease. Mr. Chau Thanh Tu, Chief Pharmacist of the Pharmaceutical Professional Council at Long Chau Pharmacy and Vaccination Center, said that the unit is preparing the necessary steps to bring the vaccine to serve the Vietnamese people as soon as possible. According to Mr. Tu, vaccination is one of the important preventive measures against infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. During the period when children return to school, in addition to the risk of hand, foot, and mouth disease, parents also need to proactively prevent easily transmissible diseases such as meningococcal disease, measles, influenza, chickenpox, and whooping cough, ensuring their children receive all vaccinations on schedule after consulting with a specialist. Until hand, foot, and mouth disease vaccines are widely available, personal hygiene, environmental disinfection, infection control, and early recognition of signs of worsening symptoms remain the most important measures. You may also like With high infection rates and young children returning to in-person learning environments, coordination between families, schools, and the health sector will be crucial in breaking the chain of transmission and limiting the number of severe cases. For families with young children, early recognition of abnormal signs is crucial in limiting complications. Parents need to closely monitor the disease's progression, avoid self-medication, and take their children to a medical facility immediately if warning signs appear. Children with hand, foot, and mouth disease should stay home from school, limit contact with other children, and follow infection prevention measures as instructed by health authorities. The health sector also advises schools and preschools to strengthen hygiene in classrooms, toys, and living equipment, and proactively identify children showing symptoms of suspected illness. Close cooperation between families, schools, and health facilities will help limit the risk of outbreaks in the school environment. supplementary_news.content: ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. — Orange County Mosquito Control officials are preparing to take to the air to fight the spread of dengue fever, as more locally acquired cases are discovered in Apopka. The latest cases bring the total number of locally acquired infections in Central Florida to five. Health officials are also investigating two additional suspected cases as concerns grow about the mosquito-borne illness. Orange County Mosquito Control Manager Steve Harrison is asking county commissioners for $150,000 to fund aerial spraying aimed at reducing the mosquito population and stopping the spread. According to the Florida Department of Health , two new locally acquired cases were identified in Apopka. “That there are two additional locally acquired cases of dengue, that brought us from the three known to now, the two additional, which gives us five. There are also two suspect cases that are being tested,” Harrison said. Harrison went before county commissioners Tuesday to request funding for the aerial spraying operation. When approved, the effort is expected to launch from Bartow on Friday, using a plane similar to the aircraft shown by mosquito control officials. The spraying would target three areas in Central Florida, and around Orange County. Harrison said aerial mosquito spraying is a routine practice during Florida’s mosquito season and should not alarm residents. “Aerial applications are nothing residents need to be concerned about. This is a common daily occurrence within the state of Florida, if not in other states as well. During the mosquito season, on any given night somewhere in the state, there is an aerial application taking place,” Harrison said. Florida has reported 296 locally acquired dengue fever cases in 2026, according to state health department surveillance data. The outbreak is concentrated in Hillsborough County, which accounts for 259 of those cases. The statewide total is among the highest reported by any U.S. state in decades. Mosquito control officials say reducing the population of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can spread dengue, is key to interrupting transmission. “We’re trying to bring down the population of Aedes aegypti, which is the primary vector for dengue, because we want to interrupt that transmission cycle. And that’s going to give us the best, public health protection to residents,” Harrison said. State health officials have also confirmed a dengue-related death in Hillsborough County. The patient’s identity has not been publicly released. Orange County Mosquito Control is asking county leaders to approve $150,000 to carry out the planned aerial spraying over Orange County

Facebook Twitter Bluesky WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter Bluesky WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save For a state whose government officially doesn’t believe climate change is real, Florida remains our nation’s busiest climate-change laboratory. The latest test for the Sunshine State is an outbreak of dengue fever, the largest in the U.S. since the 1940s. The numbers are relatively small: 485 cases as of the latest count from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, largely concentrated in Tampa’s home county. But any case of the disease — sometimes called “break-bone fever” because of how it makes sufferers’ bones feel — was rare in the U.S. not long ago. It’s too soon to attribute this particular episode to climate change because Florida can certainly be hot enough for a dengue outbreak under any circumstances. But a warming planet is making broader swaths of the planet friendlier to disease-carrying mosquitoes, which spread dengue fever. Florida’s experience today will be an example for places at higher latitudes in the near future. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes that spread dengue are most dangerous in sustained temperatures of 26 to 31 degrees Celsius (79 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a study published this week in the journal Science Advances by researchers from Monash University in Australia. These insects also love high humidity and rainfall (though they can also deal with drought because it means people keep more open containers of water). Florida has always been hot and humid. And the U.S. struggled repeatedly with dengue-like outbreaks before World War II.(Dengue wasn't isolated as a disease until 1943, though it certainly existed long before that.) But a global effort to end yellow fever quashed many mosquito-borne illnesses here for generations. Dengue didn’t return to Florida until 2009, when a handful of people caught it in Key West. Since then, the state has been the mainland’s runaway dengue leader, with 606 locally acquired cases and nearly 4,200 travel-associated cases between 2010 and 2025, according to the CDC. Second on the list is California, with nearly 2,600 mostly travel-related cases. None of them approach Puerto Rico, with more than 42,000 cases. But there’s plenty of time to start gaining ground. As my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Lara Williams has documented many times, global heating has expanded the territory of the mosquitoes that carry dengue, malaria, chikungunya, Zika and other diseases. Dengue was endemic to just nine countries 50 years ago. Now it’s in 140. A hotter planet is also boosting the numbers and range of ticks that carry Lyme, encephalitis, anaplasmosis and other horrors. And the hotter the planet gets, the more land these pests can conquer. Even under less-than-extreme greenhouse-gas emissions scenarios, the number of humans at risk of dengue will be 2.3 billion greater in 2080 than in 2015, according to the Monash study. That means 6.1 billion people, roughly the entire global population in 2000, will be regularly exposed to the disease by 2080. But human behavior and climate-change effects also reinforce each other. The steady rush of people into hot places like Florida and Texas helps explain the recent and expected future rise in dengue exposure, the Monash study noted. The (justified) end of widespread DDT spraying gave mosquitoes another tiny toehold. That means people also have the means to fight back, as we learned with yellow fever. Decades of education and billions of dollars of investment in prevention and treatment have helped slow the scourge of malaria, the global incidence rate of which fell by more than a third between 2000 and 2016, while the death rate fell by 60% (though population growth means the number of malaria cases is still rising). Increasing urbanization and economic well-being also help curb that disease. “Houston should be a malaria zone,” Columbia University professor Jeffrey Shaman, a climatologist and infectious-disease specialist who studies mosquito-borne diseases, told me. “It’s swampy, warm, and has lots of opportunities for mosquitoes to do their thing. But they don’t, and the reason is development.” But the Aedes mosquitoes actually thrive in urban environments, Shaman and the Monash study pointed out. Fighting dengue will require different weapons. Alphabet Inc.’s Google, Monash University’s World Mosquito Program and other groups have programs to infect and release mosquitoes with a bacteria called wolbachia, which can curb bug populations, at least temporarily. The Environmental Protection Agency has been sitting for months on a Google request to release infected mosquitoes in California and Florida. But President Donald Trump last week ordered his government to speed up any efforts to rein in all the mosquito- and tick-borne diseases terrorizing boggy Washington, DC, and eventually the rest of the country, which could help. Florida is already running its own experiments. Lee County, home of Fort Myers, has been releasing wolbachia-infected mosquitoes since 2017, the Miami Herald reported. It’s also using radiation to sterilize male bugs and delivering them to unsuspecting mates by plane and drone. The county currently has just 11 dengue cases, though it’s 120 miles south of Tampa. Wolbachia isn’t a perfect solution and isn’t effective everywhere. People also tend to get weirded out by the idea of Frankensquitoes buzzing around, as the Florida Keys discovered when it proposed using genetically modified bugs to curb populations. The best approach, then, is all of the above, as Williams has written. That starts with slowing down mosquito-friendly global heating. And it includes surveillance and warning systems to go along with bacteria, radiation, drones, (safe) pesticides, mosquito-eating fish and whatever else is handy. People need to get in the habit of drying out bird baths and other water containers where mosquitoes breed. Anything that gives humans and mosquitoes fewer chances to interact is worth trying, Shaman said. “That’s the name of the game for controlling outbreaks.” And if it works in Florida, it’s worth trying anywhere. Mark Gongloff is a Bloomberg Opinion editor and columnist covering climate change. He previously worked for Fortune.com, the Huffington Post and the Wall Street Journal. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Medical Even young, healthy people can go into dengue shock after their fever subsides. Many people with dengue fever mistakenly believe that the absence of fever means they are cured, when in fact this could be the time when dangerous complications begin to appear. Báo Đầu tư•11/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever continues to circulate in many localities, posing a risk of severe complications if patients are not monitored and treated promptly. Worryingly, many people are complacent about the initial symptoms, self-treating at home or assuming the disease has subsided after their body temperature returns to normal. According to a report from the Hanoi Center for Disease Control (CDC), from September 25th to the present, the city has recorded 350 cases of dengue fever in 81 wards and communes. Cumulatively from the beginning of the year to the time of this report, Hanoi has had 3,946 cases in 119 wards and communes, with 177 outbreaks recorded, of which 35 are active. Blood concentration - a serious complication of dengue fever. According to Dr. Ngo Van An, Deputy Head of the Internal Medicine Department at MEDLATEC General Hospital, one of the difficulties in detecting and treating dengue fever is that the initial symptoms are easily confused with seasonal flu or other common viral infections. Patients often experience high fever, headache, body aches, and fatigue, leading them to self-medicate without proper examination and testing to determine the cause. Meanwhile, dengue fever becomes particularly dangerous during the period from the 3rd to the 7th day after onset. This is when the patient's fever may subside, but they simultaneously enter a phase of risk for plasma leakage, circulatory disorders, and shock. The case of female patient NVP (24 years old, residing in Hanoi) who was recently admitted to MEDLATEC General Hospital is a typical example. The patient had dengue fever for 6 days, having previously self-tested at home, used a fever-reducing medication containing paracetamol (Efferalgan 500 mg), and drank oral rehydration solution (Oresol). However, just one day after the fever subsided, the patient suddenly felt weak, dizzy, and lightheaded. Noticing the unusual condition, the family quickly took the patient to the hospital for emergency treatment. Upon admission, the patient presented with significant hemodynamic instability, a rapid pulse exceeding 110 beats/minute, and a drop in blood pressure to 80/50 mmHg. Laboratory results showed an elevated hematocrit (HCT) of 43.1%, higher than the laboratory's reference range of 37-42%. HCT is an index reflecting the percentage of red blood cell volume in the blood. In people with dengue fever, this index is elevated, especially when it is higher than the baseline value, which may suggest blood concentration due to plasma leakage. However, the results need to be evaluated in conjunction with clinical manifestations and other indicators to determine the severity of the disease. Upon examination and testing, the doctors diagnosed the patient with severe Dengue hemorrhagic fever, circulatory disturbance, and a risk of hypovolemic shock. The treatment team promptly resuscitated the patient, administered intravenous fluids and electrolytes, used high-molecular-weight fluids as prescribed, and closely monitored hemodynamic and blood gas parameters. After approximately 6 hours of treatment, the patient's blood pressure improved to 120/70 mmHg, heart rate stabilized at 70 beats/minute, and HCT decreased to 39%. Having passed the immediate critical stage, the patient continued to receive inpatient treatment and intensive monitoring. Doctors say this case shows that young people without underlying medical conditions can still experience severe complications from dengue fever. In particular, the absence of fever does not always mean the disease is cured. In critical cases, the Dengue virus can increase vascular permeability, causing plasma to leak out of the blood vessels and reducing circulating volume. If this plasma leakage becomes severe and goes undetected and untreated, the patient is at risk of hypotension, shock, organ damage, and life-threatening conditions. It is noteworthy that these changes can occur while body temperature has already decreased, making it easy for patients and their families to lower their guard. Some cases initially present only with symptoms of fatigue, dizziness, abdominal pain, or vomiting, but circulatory disorders quickly develop afterward. You may also like According to experts, anyone with dengue fever is at risk of developing severe symptoms. However, certain groups require particularly close monitoring due to their potential for complications or difficulties in treatment. For the elderly and those with underlying conditions such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or chronic kidney disease, monitoring for dengue fever is often more complicated. Symptoms may be atypical, manifesting as significant fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, confusion, or altered state of consciousness. For patients using anticoagulants or other medications for chronic diseases, doctors need to carefully assess the risk of bleeding, circulatory status, and appropriate treatment options. Patients should not stop or adjust their medication without professional guidance. Young children, especially those under one year old, also need close monitoring because they cannot clearly describe bodily abnormalities. Signs such as unusual crying, refusal to feed, lethargy, cold hands and feet, or decreased urine output should be noted. Overweight or obese children with dengue fever also need careful evaluation. For pregnant women, dengue fever can increase the risk of complications for both mother and fetus, requiring examination and monitoring at an appropriate medical facility. For young, healthy individuals, the biggest risk lies in complacency. The ability to function relatively normally in the initial days or feel better after the fever subsides does not rule out the possibility of the illness progressing to a dangerous stage. Doctors advise that people with dengue fever should be especially vigilant if they experience any of the following signs: extreme fatigue, lethargy, restlessness, or unusual anxiety; severe or persistent abdominal pain, especially in the right lower rib area; frequent vomiting; bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or irregular or heavy menstrual bleeding. More serious symptoms such as vomiting blood, passing black or bloody stools, urinating very little or not urinating for hours, cold extremities, dizziness, or fainting may indicate blood loss, decreased circulating volume, or hemodynamic instability. Patients experiencing any warning signs should seek medical attention immediately, without waiting for the fever to return or for a follow-up appointment. If symptoms such as fainting, difficulty breathing, altered consciousness, significant bleeding, or signs of shock occur, immediate emergency care is required. Besides monitoring the disease progression, proper medication use plays a crucial role in limiting complications. Currently, there is no specific drug routinely used to eliminate the Dengue virus. Treatment mainly focuses on supportive care, appropriate fluid replacement, close monitoring of clinical and laboratory indicators, and early detection of signs of plasma leakage, bleeding, or organ damage. According to MEDLATEC experts, people should not self-medicate with aspirin, ibuprofen, and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to reduce fever and pain in cases of suspected or confirmed dengue fever, as these drugs can increase the risk of bleeding. Corticosteroids should not be used to treat dengue fever without a doctor's prescription. Paracetamol can be used to reduce fever at appropriate doses, but it is necessary to follow the instructions regarding dosage and intervals between doses to avoid the risk of overdose causing liver damage. Drinking oral rehydration solution (ORS) and supplementing fluids can help replenish lost fluids in patients who are conscious, able to drink, and do not have severe symptoms. However, oral rehydration does not replace assessment and treatment at a hospital if signs of plasma leakage, hypotension, or shock have appeared. Patients should also not self-administer intravenous fluids at home. You may also like Alongside treatment, preventive measures need to be maintained regularly. People should eliminate stagnant water sources, cover household water containers tightly, maintain environmental hygiene, kill mosquito larvae, and take measures to prevent mosquito bites, even during the day. Given the evolving situation with Dengue fever, doctors emphasize that monitoring patients during the fever-reduction phase is particularly important. Early detection of abnormalities in circulation, consciousness, bleeding, and urine output can help patients receive intervention before complications become serious. According to preventive medicine experts, proactive disease prevention is especially important, and vaccination is one of the effective solutions for infectious diseases for which vaccines are available. Regarding dengue fever, according to doctors at the Long Chau Vaccination System, Vietnam uses the Qdenga dengue vaccine. This vaccine is administered to children aged 4 and older and adults, including those who have previously had the disease, and helps prevent all four types of the Dengue virus. The vaccination schedule consists of two doses, administered three months apart. The protective efficacy is over 80%, reducing the risk of hospitalization due to dengue fever by over 90% when the full vaccination regimen is completed. Experts believe the greatest significance of the vaccine lies not only in reducing the risk of contracting the disease but also in limiting severe cases, easing the burden on the healthcare system during outbreaks, and contributing to the protection of high-risk groups such as children. However, the vaccine is not suitable for people who are hypersensitive to any of its components, pregnant women, or breastfeeding mothers. For immunocompromised individuals or those with HIV, please consult a healthcare professional for guidance tailored to your specific situation. supplementary_news.content: LIVE TV POLITICSTÜRKİYEWAR ON GAZABIZTECHINFOGRAPHICSFEATURESOPINIONWAR ON IRAN HEALTH & EDUCATION 1 min read What is dengue virus? Also known as “breakbone fever,” dengue is a viral disease transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Share Producer: Hatice Cagla Gunaydin, Graphic Artist: Busra Ozturk / TRT World More than 2.2 million dengue cases and nearly 1,200 deaths were reported across 97 countries and territories in the first eight months of 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). In October, Bangladesh's reported total surpassed 103,000 cases and 300 deaths, while Cuba has recorded 11,235 cases so far in 2026. Florida is also experiencing the largest dengue outbreak in any US state in decades, with nearly 300 locally acquired cases reported this year. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Restaurants Real Estate Opinion Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Two new cases of dengue fever found in Florida; aerial spray planned The two new confirmed cases are in the Apopka area of Orange County. Michelle Spitzer USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 13, 2026, 12:14 p.m. ET Florida has reported 298 cases of dengue fever, the largest outbreak in the state in decades. Hillsborough County has the most reported cases, while Orange County is planning aerial spraying to combat mosquitoes. The surge is attributed to warmer temperatures, increased rainfall, and travel from countries with outbreaks. Two new cases of dengue fever, the mosquito-borne illnesses spreading throughout the state, were reported in one Florida county. The Florida Department of Health confirmed the two additional cases in the Apopka area, Orange County officials announced Oct. 12. This brings the statewide total to 298. “We are planning to aerial spray over the next two to three weeks,” Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control said in a press release. “We will be spraying in the Apopka and Pine Hills areas to kill the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which is the known carrier of Dengue.” Orange County now has a total of five cases. Aerial spraying is expected to reduce the targeted mosquito population by 99%, according to Harrison. “It is very important for residents to ensure that there is no standing water on their property,” Harrison said. “We encourage residents to walk around their yards after a storm and drain any standing water, toss out anything that could hold water, and protect yourself with long sleeves, pants, and EPA-approved mosquito repellent.” What Florida county has the most reported dengue fever cases? Hillsborough County has most of the cases, with 259 reported as of Oct. 3, according to the Florida Department of Health. Other counties with reported cases are Pinellas (20), Miami-Dade (8), Orange (5), Pasco (3), Broward (1) Palm Beach (1) and Polk (1). This year’s 298 cases is the largest outbreak in decades. The previous highest number in Florida was 199 in 2023. Last year, 62 cases were reported in the state. Three Tampa Bay-area counties — Pasco, Hillsborough, and Pinellas — have declared states of emergency to expedite mosquito control operations and cut through paperwork for emergency response. What's causing the Florida outbreak of dengue fever? One reason for the surge in dengue cases is because of a combination of "climatic and human factors that create ideal conditions" for the types of mosquitoes that spread dengue, West Nile and the chikungunya viruses, said Eva Buckner, associate professor and extension specialist with the UF/IFAS Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory via email Sept. 23. Those factors include warmer temperatures, increased rainfall and standing water, and human travel from other countries with outbreaks. Health data show that 215 of the 262 Florida cases acquired from outside the country were people who had recently traveled from Cuba. Most of the cases were DENV-2, one of the disease's four serotypes and the serotype behind Cuba's current epidemic, where fuel shortages are hampering fumigation efforts, according to Forbes. What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. C.A. supplementary_news.content: Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle LifestyleFlorida has seen more dengue cases than it has in decades Health Florida has seen more dengue cases than it has in decades The range of mosquitoes that transmit the dengue virus continues to expand. (Featured image) Keystone The state of Florida is currently reporting more cases of dengue fever than it has in decades. An elderly woman died after contracting dengue fever. Keystone-SDA 13.10.2026, 05:32 According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), more than 500 cases have already been reported this year, including about 280 local transmissions. The remaining cases occurred during travel. The majority of cases are reported in the area surrounding the Tampa metropolitan area, where an elderly woman died in September after contracting dengue fever. Several municipalities in the region have declared a state of emergency. Also known as “bone-breaking disease” Dengue fever—sometimes called “breakbone fever” because of the pain it causes—is transmitted by certain species of mosquitoes and is widespread in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection with the virus can cause symptoms such as high fever, nausea, and severe headaches and body aches, but in most cases, the illness resolves without lasting effects. In a small percentage of cases, a severe, potentially life-threatening form of the disease develops. Local dengue outbreaks are not unusual in Florida—but on this scale, they certainly are. The highest number of cases to date was recorded in 2023, when there were just under 200. Because the range of the mosquitoes that transmit these diseases continues to expand, an increasing number of local infections are now being reported even outside the tropics and subtropics. In Europe, according to the EU health agency ECDC, Italy and France have reported such local infections so far this year. To date, no locally transmitted cases of tropical diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, or Zika fever carried by tiger mosquitoes have been recorded in Switzerland, as the Federal Council announced in late September. Article will play after ad... Playing in :00 A A A Kaua‘i mosquito trapping (Aug. 25, 2022). PC: Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources The Hawai‘i Department of Health reports identifying a new travel-related dengue virus case on Oʻahu, bringing the total number of dengue cases in the state to eight for 2026. All of the cases have involved travel to Pacific Island countries and territories. The affected individual was exposed to the virus while traveling in a region where dengue is common. No connection to any prior cases in Hawaiʻi have been found. Health department teams have been deployed to conduct inspections and implement mosquito control measures in the affected area. Dengue virus is transmitted from an infected person to a mosquito and then to another person. Due to the circumstances of this case, the expected risk of transmission is low. However, with recent heavy rain, this case is a reminder for the public to eliminate standing water as much as possible. Reducing standing water helps prevent mosquito breeding and can reduce the risk of local transmission of vector-borne diseases. More information about mosquito control is available on the Vector Control Branch website. Dengue is a year-round risk in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, including Brazil and Mexico; Asia, including the Philippines; the Middle East; Africa; and several Pacific islands, including American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations in the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are also affected. Some countries are reporting higher-than-usual numbers of dengue cases, including Bangladesh, Bolivia, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Kenya, Malaysia, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Panama, Sri Lanka, Vanuatu and Vietnam. Travelers should review current, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. For current travel health information and guidance, visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) travel website. Anyone planning to travel to or who has recently visited an area with dengue risk may be at risk for infection. The CDC advises travelers to take standard precautions when visiting such areas. These include using an Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long pants outdoors, as well as sleeping in air-conditioned rooms, rooms with window screens or under insecticide-treated bed nets. Travelers returning from areas with dengue risk should take precautions to prevent mosquito bites for three weeks. If dengue symptoms develop within two weeks of returning, travelers should seek medical evaluation. Symptoms of dengue can range from mild to severe and include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash and body aches. Symptoms typically last two to seven days. While severe illness can occur, most people recover within a week. Individuals who have recently traveled and are experiencing these symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Healthcare providers and individuals who suspect dengue infection are advised to call the Disease Reporting Line at 808-586-4586. In areas with suspected or confirmed dengue cases, Health Department vector control personnel conduct inspections and mosquito-reduction activities. Reducing mosquito populations lowers the risk of dengue transmission to others. In areas without reported dengue cases, eliminating mosquito breeding sites around the home is an important preventive measure. Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water to breed. Common breeding sites include buckets, water-catching plants such as bromeliads, small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside. Prevent standing water from collecting around homes and workplaces by emptying containers and other items where mosquitoes can lay eggs. Home News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod News Region Girl, 8, dies of severe dengue in Bacolod By Mae Singuay - Thursday, October 15, 2026 Facebook X Viber Print BACOLOD City — An eight-year-old girl from Barangay Handumanan died of severe dengue, bringing the city’s dengue-related fatalities to six as infections increased by 1.5 percent from last year’s figure, the City Health Office (CHO) reported. The child died on October 3 after suffering complications, including dengue hemorrhagic shock, pulmonary hemorrhage and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. She was admitted to a hospital on October 1 after experiencing persistent fever, vomiting and abdominal pain, followed by diarrhea. According to the CHO, the girl had previously been hospitalized for dengue at the age of five, making her latest infection her second encounter with the mosquito-borne disease. She developed a high fever on September 28, which temporarily subsided after she was given paracetamol. She initially consulted a private clinic and was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection before her condition worsened. Laboratory results on October 1 showed that her platelet count had dropped to 34,000, indicating a dangerously low level. Despite hospitalization, her condition continued to deteriorate, and she suffered cardiopulmonary arrest on October 3. She was pronounced dead at around 10:30 a.m. Discover more Regional news subscription Western Visayas news Local event coverage The CHO said the fatality was reported to the office on October 4. The latest death brings to six the number of dengue-related fatalities recorded in Bacolod as of Morbidity Week 39, covering September 27 to October 3. The city recorded 891 dengue cases during the period, up 1.5 percent from the 878 cases reported during the same period in 2025. The number of deaths remained unchanged at six. The other fatalities involved a nine-year-old boy and a four-year-old girl from Barangay Mansilingan, an eight-year-old boy from Barangay 16, a five-year-old girl from Barangay Granada, and an eight-year-old girl from Barangay Villamonte. CHO records showed that Barangay Mansilingan had the highest number of dengue cases, with 105, followed by Handumanan with 77 and Estefania with 73. Other barangays with high case counts were Alijis, with 58; Granada, 55; Villamonte and Taculing, 54 each; Singcang-Airport, 53; Tangub, 44; and Banago, 39. Dr. Grace Tan, head of the CHO’s Environmental Sanitation Division, urged residents experiencing fever and flu-like symptoms to seek early medical consultation. She also reminded the public to remain vigilant against dengue and follow the Department of Health’s 4S strategy: search for and destroy mosquito-breeding sites; secure self-protection against mosquito bites; seek early consultation; and support fogging and spraying in areas where these are warranted. Meanwhile, CHO Assistant Department Head Dr. Grace Tan also emphasized the importance of sustained household and community efforts to eliminate mosquito-breeding grounds. Residents were encouraged to practice the city’s “4Ts” of dengue prevention: Taob, Taktak, Tuyo and Takip — turn over water containers, discard accumulated water, keep containers dry, and cover water-storage vessels. The city also urged households to participate in its daily 4 p.m. cleanup habit to remove stagnant water and other potential mosquito-breeding sites. Health authorities advised residents to watch for dengue symptoms, including sudden high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pain, pain behind the eyes, weakness and skin rashes. Discover more Environment news report Health wellness tips Business news updates Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, dark-colored stools and difficulty breathing are warning signs that require immediate medical attention. The CHO stressed that dengue can progress rapidly and become life-threatening, making early consultation, close monitoring and prompt medical intervention essential to preventing severe complications and deaths./PN RELATED ARTICLESMORE FROM AUTHOR Region Bacolod releases P13.6M MassKara subsidies for participating barangays, schools Region Woman’s body found in sack in Talisay; 2 suspects arrested Region Molo lodging house room boy dies; police rule out foul play LEAVE A REPLY Cancel reply Please enter your comment! trained doctors and healthcare professionals from public hospitals and treatment facilities on dengue case management ISLAMABAD, Oct 09 (APP):The World Health Organization (WHO) has trained doctors and healthcare professionals from public hospitals and treatment facilities on dengue case management The focus of the training is on updated clinical guidance, early detection and timely treatment to prevent severe complications and save lives. The training aimed to strengthen healthcare professionals’ capacity to identify dengue symptoms, monitor warning signs and provide appropriate clinical care in line with updated recommendations and global best practices. Emphasizing the importance of preparedness and early intervention, WHO highlighted that timely diagnosis, close monitoring of patients and prompt management of warning signs were essential to reducing the risk of severe dengue and improving patient outcomes. The initiative underscores the importance of strengthening clinical capacity and ensuring effective management of dengue cases, particularly during periods of increased transmission. supplementary_news.content: newsinfo / Metro Metro Manila records 23 new dengue cases; total hits 3,822 By: Cristina Eloisa Baclig - Content Researcher Writer / @inquirerdotnet INQUIRER.net / 03:39 PM October 12, 2026 INQUIRER FILES MANILA, Philippines—Manila recorded 23 new dengue cases on Monday, bringing the total number of cases reported in the city from Jan. 1 to Oct. 12 to 3,822, according to the Manila Health Department (MHD). The department’s latest W.I.L.D. (water- and food-borne diseases, influenza, leptospirosis, and dengue) diseases report also listed 19 new cases of influenza-like illness (ILI) and four cases of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI). No new cases of cholera, typhoid fever, confirmed COVID-19, or leptospirosis were reported on Oct. 12. LEARN MORE » Sections বাংলা Thursday, October 15, 2026 Today's Paper Video e-Paper Second Edition Contact Sections Home Frontpage Asia City World OP-ED Editorial Business Global Business Commercial Capital Sports Countrywide Featured Sex & Relationship Student Voice LitScape Life Style Reciprocal Teens & Twenties In Vogue Food & Nutrition Bookshelf Entertainment Back Page × Facebook Twitter Pinterest Home Frontpage Published: 01:04 AM, 10 October 2026 Health experts urge early testing, timely treatment to reduce dengue deaths Observing that most dengue deaths are linked to delayed diagnosis and hospitalisation, health experts have called for early testing, timely treatment and greater public awareness of the disease's warning signs to help reduce fatalities from the mosquito-borne illness. They said many dengue patients who die in hospitals arrive at a late stage, leaving doctors with little time to provide effective treatment. "Most of the patients reach us so late that we hardly get time to provide treatment. They arrive in an irreversible condition and, unfortunately, we cannot save them," said Professor Shahnoor Sharmin Munni, head of the Dengue Unit at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH), BSS reports. Discover more Get Health Tips health Health She said many people still believe dengue testing should be done only after three days of fever, while some become less alert when the fever subsides. "In dengue, a patient may become seriously ill after the fever comes down. Many people remain at home thinking that the danger has passed, but the patient may actually go into shock at that stage," Prof Munni said. She identified three key areas of public awareness: when to undergo dengue testing, what to do when fever subsides and how to recognise warning signs. She added that greater awareness could help narrow the gap between the onset of complications and receiving medical care. Echoing Prof Munni, Mugda Medical College Hospital (MMCH) Deputy Director Dr Muhammad Nurul Islam urged people to seek medical attention as soon as fever develops and get tested if dengue is suspected. He said dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, often begins with sudden high fever, body aches, weakness and loss of appetite and warned that a fall in fever after two or three days should not necessarily be considered a sign of recovery. "In dengue, the most dangerous complication is plasma leakage, which can continue even after the fever subsides," Dr Islam said. According to him, plasma leakage causes the fluid component of blood to move out of the blood vessels, reducing circulating blood volume. If the loss becomes significant, a patient can develop shock, characterised by a weak or undetectable pulse, low blood pressure and severe weakness, he said. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Grief Support Death "Without timely intervention, the condition can become fatal," he said. Calling for early diagnosis, Dr Islam said different tests can be useful at different stages of the illness, including the NS1 antigen test in the early phase and antibody tests such as IgM and IgG at later stages. "If dengue can be detected at an early stage, most cases can be managed at home under the national guidelines and do not necessarily require hospital admission," he said. Regarding treatment, the physician said many dengue cases can be managed with adequate rest, nutritious food and sufficient oral fluids, along with paracetamol for fever and body aches. Patients should continue to get adequate rest and drink suitable fluids such as water, lemon drinks, coconut water, fruit juice and soup even after the fever subsides, he said, warning that returning to strenuous physical activities immediately after fever comes down could be risky if plasma leakage is continuing. Dr Islam strongly advised against taking antibiotics or other painkillers without medical advice, saying antibiotics act against bacterial infections, whereas dengue is caused by a virus. "There is no role for antibiotics in treating dengue itself," he said, urging patients to consult registered physicians and follow national treatment guidelines. Dr Islam also cautioned against taking painkillers other than paracetamol, saying drugs such as aspirin and some other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can increase the risk of bleeding, particularly when platelet counts are low. Discover more Find Treatments Seek Counseling Find Hospitals Warning signs of severe dengue include bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in the stool or vomit, abnormal vaginal bleeding and bleeding under the skin, Dr Islam said. On fluid therapy, he stressed that oral and intravenous (IV) fluids should not be treated in the same way, saying IV fluids should only be administered under the supervision of a registered physician. "Both too little and too much fluid can be dangerous," he said, explaining that inadequate fluid replacement can contribute to shock, while excessive IV fluid can cause fluid overload and potentially lead to heart failure. Kurmitola Multicare Specialized Hospital (KMSH) Director Brigadier General Md Saydur Rahman also encouraged early diagnosis, saying not every dengue patient requires hospital admission if the disease is detected at an early stage. Only around 10 to 15 percent of patients with more serious symptoms, including bleeding, severe diarrhoea or vomiting that cannot be controlled, require hospitalisation, he said. Observing that low platelet counts and plasma leakage have traditionally been major concerns in dengue cases, Saydur Rahman said doctors are now seeing more patients with cardiac and liver-related complications. Such complications can sometimes become life-threatening, he said, urging people to seek treatment as soon as possible. Meanwhile, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) Director (Hospital and Clinics) Dr Md Nurul Islam said adequate quantities of dengue diagnostic kits and intravenous fluids, particularly saline, are currently available at hospitals up to the upazila level across the country. The government is therefore encouraging people to seek testing at local health facilities as soon as possible after developing fever so that dengue can be identified early and appropriate treatment can begin without delay, he said. "There is no fixed rule that a dengue test must be conducted only after three days of fever. We are advising people to get tested as early as possible, depending on the clinical situation," Dr Nurul Islam said. Early treatment can reduce pressure on major hospitals in Dhaka and other large cities, as patients can receive appropriate care at nearby upazila health complexes, district hospitals and medical college hospitals, he added. According to the DGHS, a total of 94,151 people have so far been infected with dengue across the country while 294 died of the disease this year.
